parts.title: Living on the Ring of Fire: Japan and Its Earthquakes
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Japan's relationship with earthquakes is not an occasional misfortune but a permanent condition of life. The archipelago lies where several tectonic plates collide and slide beneath one another, producing well over a thousand tremors that people actually feel each year and a share of the world's most powerful earthquakes that is out of all proportion to the country's size, commonly estimated at around a fifth.

Its history is marked by catastrophe. The Great Kanto earthquake of 1923, which struck the Tokyo region at lunchtime, killed more than one hundred thousand people, most of them in the fires that swept through wooden neighborhoods. In 1995 the Kobe earthquake killed some six thousand, and in 2011 a magnitude 9.0 quake off the northeast coast generated a tsunami that left roughly eighteen thousand people dead or missing and triggered the nuclear accident at Fukushima Daiichi. Each disaster exposed a different weakness, and each prompted a different reform.

The most visible reform concerns buildings. Japan overhauled its seismic standards in 1981, requiring buildings to survive strong shaking without collapsing, and when Kobe was struck fourteen years later, damage was heavily concentrated among older buildings that **predated** the rules. Since then, engineers have developed techniques such as base isolation, in which a structure rests on flexible bearings that absorb ground movement, and tall towers are fitted with dampers that counteract swaying. The result is that a quake which would flatten poorly built housing elsewhere may leave a Tokyo skyscraper largely undamaged.

Technology offers a second layer of defense. Since 2007, the Japan Meteorological Agency has operated a nationwide early-warning system that detects the fast but relatively harmless primary waves of an earthquake and broadcasts an alert before the slower, more destructive waves arrive. **The warning** may come only seconds in advance, and people close to the epicenter may receive none at all, yet even a few seconds are enough to halt high-speed trains, stop elevators at the nearest floor, and let individuals drop beneath a desk. Occasional false alarms are accepted as the price of speed.

Less visible, but arguably as important, is a culture of preparedness. Every September 1, the anniversary of the 1923 disaster, schools, offices, and neighborhoods hold drills, and many households keep emergency bags beside the door. Along the northeast coast, old stone markers warn descendants not to build below certain points, advice that was sometimes ignored as memories faded. The experience of 2011 reinforced the lesson: in the town of Kamaishi, most schoolchildren who had practiced evacuating on their own initiative reached high ground, an outcome that educators now cite worldwide.

Preparedness has limits, however, as the Noto Peninsula earthquake of January 1, 2024 demonstrated. The magnitude 7.6 quake struck a region with an ageing population and many older wooden houses, and damaged roads left villages cut off for days, slowing relief. Not only did the disaster reveal how unevenly resilience is distributed between cities and rural areas, but it also raised doubts about whether plans designed around large urban centers can serve shrinking communities. Meanwhile, the government's warning that a major quake along the Nankai Trough is likely within thirty years, a risk it has put at roughly eighty percent, keeps the question urgent.

Đọc câu chủ đề và nắm mạch lập luận xuyên suốt toàn bài: các đoạn đầu giới thiệu bối cảnh địa chấn ở Nhật Bản và các lớp phòng vệ (quy chuẩn xây dựng kháng chấn, kỹ thuật cách ly chấn động/bộ giảm chấn); các đoạn giữa bàn về hệ thống cảnh báo sớm, văn hóa chuẩn bị ứng phó của cộng đồng và hộ gia đình; các đoạn cuối phân tích những giới hạn bộc lộ qua các trận động đất lớn và thách thức ở các khu vực nông thôn/lão hóa dân số. Phương án đúng cần bao quát trọn vẹn việc Nhật Bản xây dựng nhiều lớp phòng vệ nhưng các sự kiện gần đây vẫn phơi bày giới hạn của chúng, tránh các đáp án quy chụp vùng nông thôn an toàn hơn đô thị, coi cảnh báo sớm là giải pháp duy nhất toàn cầu hay cho rằng quy chuẩn đã xóa sổ thương vong.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R3Q1, R3Q4, R3Q9):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Scanning** (Đọc quét từ khóa đặc hiệu) để đối chiếu thông tin trực tiếp trong từng đoạn được chỉ định.
  - Với **R3Q1**, quét tên trận động đất "Kobe" và mốc "1981" ở đoạn 3 để xác định mức độ hư hại tập trung chủ yếu ở các công trình cũ xây dựng trước tiêu chuẩn năm 1981.
  - Với **R3Q4**, quét từ khóa về cảnh báo ngắn/sớm ở đoạn 4 để tìm tác dụng thực tế dù chỉ trong vài giây (như dừng tàu hỏa, ngắt hệ thống/thiết bị và giúp người dân tìm chỗ trú ẩn an toàn).
  - Với **R3Q9**, quét tên "Noto Peninsula" ở đoạn 6 để tìm tác động lên công tác cứu trợ do hạ tầng/đường sá hư hỏng khiến nhiều thôn bản bị cô lập nhiều ngày.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R3Q6):** Đối soát các nét văn hóa chuẩn bị phòng chống thiên tai được nhắc đến trong bài (như diễn tập cộng đồng hằng năm vào ngày 1/9, bia đá cổ cảnh báo giới hạn xây dựng, hay túi đồ khẩn cấp đặt gần cửa ra vào ở nhiều gia đình). Hãy loại trừ các yếu tố có xuất hiện trong bài để chọn ra khoản mục không được đề cập.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q8):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Context Clues** (Manh mối ngữ cảnh) kết hợp phân tích cấu trúc câu.
  - Với **R3Q3**, xét động từ **"predated"** ở đoạn 3 khi mô tả các công trình tồn tại trước khi quy chuẩn năm 1981 có hiệu lực; ngữ cảnh hướng tới trình tự thời gian xảy ra trước đó.
  - Với **R3Q8**, xét động từ **"counteract"** ở đoạn 3 trong ngữ cảnh kỹ thuật hoặc kết cấu làm giảm bớt lực rung lắc/tác động của động đất; chọn nghĩa tương đương với làm giảm tác động của.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R3Q5):** Xác định cụm danh từ chỉ định **"The warning"** ở đoạn 4. Đọc ngược lại các câu trước đó trong đoạn để tìm chính xác thông điệp/tín hiệu cảnh báo sớm vừa được nhắc đến làm đối tượng tham chiếu, tránh nhầm sang sóng phá hủy chậm hơn, toàn bộ hệ thống quốc gia hay sóng sơ cấp.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R3Q7):** Kết hợp thông tin từ đoạn 3 về tiêu chuẩn xây dựng/hạ tầng đô thị với đoạn 6 về khó khăn tại các khu vực nông thôn và cộng đồng dân cư già hóa. Từ hai đoạn này ghép lại, rút ra kết luận hợp lý về việc mức độ bảo vệ đạt được ở các thành phố có thể không lan tỏa đồng đều tới các vùng nông thôn đang lão hóa.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Thái độ tác giả (R3Q10):** Quan sát giọng điệu xuyên suốt bài viết khi đánh giá cách tiếp cận của Nhật Bản: tác giả đánh giá cao thành tựu kỹ thuật và ý thức phòng bị cộng đồng, đồng thời chỉ ra thẳng thắn các khoảng trống và giới hạn còn tồn tại. Hãy chọn phương án phản ánh đúng sự trân trọng nhưng thực tế này, tránh các đáp án phê phán phủ nhận, hoảng loạn cực đoan hay xem nhẹ nguy cơ.
Lời khuyên: Hãy xử lý trước nhóm câu hỏi có tọa độ rõ ràng và tập trung vào từ/cụm từ như Quy chiếu (R3Q5) và Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q8). Tiếp theo, dùng kỹ thuật đọc quét để giải quyết nhanh nhóm Chi tiết (R3Q1, R3Q4, R3Q9) và **Loại trừ NOT** (R3Q6). Cuối cùng, khi đã nắm trọn vẹn mạch thông tin và mối liên hệ giữa các đoạn, bạn sẽ dễ dàng chốt đáp án chính xác cho ba câu hỏi tổng hợp gồm **Suy luận** (R3Q7), **Thái độ tác giả** (R3Q10) và **Tóm tắt toàn** bài (R3Q2).

parts.title: Riding the Wind: How Wind Power Became an Industry
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: The modern wind industry is often described as a recent phenomenon, yet its roots reach back to the late nineteenth century. In 1887, the American inventor Charles Brush built a large machine in Cleveland that produced electricity for his mansion, and in Denmark, the teacher and inventor Poul la Cour began experiments a few years later that would eventually shape his country's industrial future. For decades, however, cheap coal and oil kept such devices at the margins.

It took a shock to change that. The oil crises of the 1970s persuaded several governments that dependence on imported fuel was a strategic weakness, and Denmark in particular began supporting domestic turbine makers, some of which grew into global firms. In California, generous tax incentives in the early 1980s triggered a rush of installations, although many early machines proved unreliable and the boom faded when the incentives expired. Lessons from **both episodes** were absorbed by the industry: technology arguably improved fastest where policy was patient.

Policy design, in fact, has often mattered as much as engineering. In 2000, Germany guaranteed generators a fixed payment for the electricity they fed into the grid, giving investors the certainty they needed and prompting a rapid expansion that other countries later imitated in various forms. More recently, many governments have replaced fixed payments with competitive auctions, in which developers bid to supply power at the lowest price. Auctions have driven costs down, but critics warn that they can also encourage unrealistically low bids that later prove impossible to honor.

The next frontier lies at sea. The first offshore wind farm, built off the Danish coast in 1991, was a small experiment, but today's offshore projects involve hundreds of turbines and investments measured in billions. **[A]** Most are anchored to the seabed, which restricts them to relatively shallow water. **[B]** Floating designs, first deployed commercially off Scotland in 2017, are intended to open deeper waters. [C] Whether they can be built cheaply enough to compete remains uncertain, and for now they account for only a tiny share of installed capacity. **[D]**

Even so, the industry's momentum has been interrupted. Rising interest rates, higher material costs, and supply-chain bottlenecks have squeezed the finances of projects whose prices were agreed years earlier, and several high-profile offshore schemes have been cancelled or renegotiated. Because wind farms require heavy upfront spending and earn their returns slowly, they are unusually sensitive to the cost of borrowing, a vulnerability that rarely features in public debate about their merits. Only when governments adjust contract terms to reflect changing conditions do stalled projects tend to move forward again.

Social acceptance is another variable that spreadsheets capture poorly. Denmark encouraged local ownership, allowing neighbors to buy shares in nearby turbines, and the resulting sense of shared benefit is often credited with easing opposition. Where communities bear the visual and acoustic costs while distant investors collect the profits, resistance tends to be stronger, a pattern that planners in many countries have been slow to **heed**. Compensation schemes and shared ownership are therefore gaining attention, though evidence about which approach works best remains mixed.

The history of wind power thus suggests a sober conclusion. The technology matured not through a single breakthrough but through decades of incremental improvement, shaped at every stage by subsidies, regulation, financing, and public attitudes. Seldom has an energy source depended so visibly on choices made outside the laboratory, and few observers expect that to change. Its future is likely to be decided as much by the quality of policy as by the size of the next generation of blades.

Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

Đọc câu chủ đề và nắm mạch lập luận xuyên suốt toàn bài: các đoạn đầu theo dấu sự phát triển của điện gió gắn với chính sách, ưu đãi và bối cảnh lịch sử; các đoạn giữa phân tích cơ chế đấu thầu cạnh tranh, giới hạn địa lý/kỹ thuật ngoài khơi (như độ sâu vùng biển) và các áp lực tài chính/chuỗi cung ứng; các đoạn cuối bàn về sự đồng thuận cộng đồng, phân bổ lợi ích - chi phí và triển vọng dài hạn. Phương án đúng cần bao quát trọn vẹn việc điện gió phát triển nhờ chính sách, tài chính và sự chấp nhận của công chúng song hành cùng công nghệ, tránh các đáp án quy chụp việc chấm dứt mở rộng vĩnh viễn, khẳng định nguồn gốc/thống trị tuyệt đối hay đặt cược vào một loại tuabin duy nhất.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q7):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Scanning** (Đọc quét từ khóa đặc hiệu) để đối chiếu thông tin trực tiếp trong từng đoạn được chỉ định.
  - Với **R4Q2**, quét từ khóa liên quan đến đấu thầu cạnh tranh ("competitive auctions") ở đoạn 3 để tìm lời phê bình về việc cơ chế này có thể thúc đẩy mức giá chào thầu thấp thiếu thực tế, dẫn đến khó thực hiện về sau.
  - Với **R4Q7**, quét từ khóa về sự phản đối trang trại gió ("resistance") ở đoạn 6 để xác định nguyên nhân gắn với sự bất cân xứng khi người dân địa phương chịu tác động/chi phí trong khi nhà đầu tư ở xa hưởng lợi nhuận.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q5):** Đối soát các yếu tố tác động tới tài chính hoặc tiến độ các dự án điện gió ngoài khơi gần đây được nêu trong bài (như lãi suất vay tăng cao, chi phí vật liệu xây dựng leo thang, hay điểm nghẽn chuỗi cung ứng làm chậm thiết bị). Hãy loại trừ các yếu tố có xuất hiện trong bài để chọn ra chi tiết không được đề cập.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q1, R4Q8):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Context Clues** (Manh mối ngữ cảnh) kết hợp phân tích cấu trúc câu.
  - Với **R4Q1**, xét động từ **"squeezed"** ở đoạn 5 khi mô tả biên lợi nhuận hoặc dự án bị chèn ép giữa chi phí tăng và giá bán/hợp đồng cố định; ngữ cảnh hướng tới việc bị đặt dưới sức ép, bị ép chặt.
  - Với **R4Q8**, xét động từ **"heed"** ở đoạn 6 trong ngữ cảnh lắng nghe hoặc lưu tâm đến ý kiến/mối quan tâm của cộng đồng địa phương; chọn nghĩa tương đương với chú ý, lưu tâm đến.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R4Q4):** Xác định cụm danh từ chỉ định **"both episodes"** ở đoạn 2. Đọc ngược lại các câu trước đó trong đoạn để tìm chính xác hai trường hợp/bối cảnh tiêu biểu vừa được nhắc đến làm đối tượng tham chiếu, tránh nhầm sang các cỗ máy đời đầu, ưu đãi thuế/lắp đặt hay các cuộc khủng hoảng dầu mỏ.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chèn câu vào đoạn văn (R4Q6):** Phân tích nội dung câu cần chèn ("Such limits are a serious obstacle for countries whose coastal waters deepen quickly, which includes much of the Pacific rim.") — câu này đòi hỏi phía trước phải nêu rõ **các giới hạn** ("Such limits") liên quan đến điều kiện triển khai/độ sâu đáy biển và nối tiếp hợp lý với các quốc gia ven biển dốc sâu ở vành đai Thái Bình Dương. Hãy đối chiếu vị trí xuất hiện các giới hạn này trong đoạn 4 để chọn ô vuông **[A]**, **[B]**, **[C]**, hoặc **[D]** khớp nhất về cả nghĩa lẫn mạch liên kết.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q9):** Kết hợp thông tin từ đoạn 3 về cơ chế hợp đồng/đấu thầu với đoạn 5 về việc chi phí và lãi suất biến động làm nhiều dự án bị đình trệ hoặc đàm phán lại. Từ hai đoạn này ghép lại, rút ra kết luận hợp lý về việc các điều khoản hợp đồng thiếu linh hoạt trước bối cảnh thay đổi có thể khiến những dự án vốn khả thi bị chững lại.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Thái độ tác giả (R4Q10):** Quan sát giọng điệu xuyên suốt bài viết khi nhìn về tương lai của điện gió: tác giả ghi nhận bước tiến và tiềm năng nhưng nhấn mạnh rằng chính sách, tài chính và tính công bằng/đồng thuận cộng đồng đóng vai trò quyết định cùng công nghệ. Hãy chọn phương án phản ánh đúng thái độ thực tế, cân bằng này, tránh các đáp án hưng phấn quá mức, thù địch hoặc bàng quan.
Lời khuyên: Hãy xử lý trước nhóm câu hỏi có tọa độ rõ ràng và tập trung vào từ/cụm từ như Quy chiếu (R4Q4) và Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q1, R4Q8). Tiếp theo, dùng kỹ thuật đọc quét để giải quyết nhanh nhóm Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q7), Loại trừ NOT (R4Q5) và Chèn câu (R4Q6). Cuối cùng, khi đã nắm trọn vẹn mạch thông tin và mối liên hệ giữa các đoạn, bạn sẽ dễ dàng chốt đáp án chính xác cho các câu hỏi tổng hợp gồm **Suy luận** (R4Q9), **Thái độ tác giả** (R4Q10) và **Ý** chính toàn bài (R4Q3).

parts.title: The Cyclo: A Vietnamese Street Icon
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: If you walk through the Old Quarter of Hanoi or the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, you may see a cyclo. A cyclo is a three-wheeled vehicle with a seat at the front for one or two passengers and a driver who sits behind and pedals. In Vietnamese, it is called xích lô, a name that comes from the French word cyclo. For many visitors, riding in one is a slow and relaxing way to see the city. Cyclos can also be found in Cambodia and some other Asian countries.

The story of the cyclo begins with an older vehicle, the rickshaw. In the late nineteenth century, the French brought hand-pulled rickshaws to Hanoi, and they quickly became a popular way for rich residents and officials to travel. Rickshaw drivers were often poor workers from the countryside, and their income depended on how far they could run. However, the work was very hard, because the driver had to run on foot while pulling the carriage. Some people felt that this was a tiring and unfair job.

In the late 1930s, a new kind of vehicle appeared. It was based on a French design, and it used a bicycle-like frame, so the driver could sit and pedal instead of running. The first cyclos arrived in Vietnam around 1939. **They** were faster and less tiring than rickshaws, and they could carry both people and goods. Many cyclos had a folding roof, which kept passengers dry during the rainy season. Soon cyclos replaced rickshaws in many cities, and they spread to Saigon and other towns.

For several decades, the cyclo was an important part of city transport. Thousands of drivers earned a living by taking passengers to markets, schools, and offices. In busy markets, cyclos were also used to carry rice, vegetables, and other goods. During the war years, many people who had lost their jobs in the countryside moved to cities and became cyclo drivers. After the war ended in 1975, however, the number of cyclos slowly fell. Motorbikes became cheaper and faster, and city governments in some places **limited** cyclos on busy roads because they moved slowly and caused traffic problems.

Today, the cyclo has found a new role. Few people use it for daily travel, but it is popular with tourists who want to enjoy the streets at a gentle speed. Some drivers now work as guides, telling visitors about local food, old buildings, and city life. In this way, the cyclo has changed from a basic means of transport into a symbol of Vietnamese culture. Some artists and photographers have also used the cyclo in their work, which helps keep its image alive. Many residents hope that it will **survive**, even though the city around it keeps changing quickly.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: How tourists in Hanoi can learn to pedal a cyclo safely
options.B: How the cyclo developed in Vietnam and what role it has today
options.C: Why rickshaws were better vehicles than cyclos for crowded Vietnamese cities
options.D: How motorbikes took over Vietnamese roads after the end of the war

questions.explanation: Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu mở đầu và nắm mạch phát triển xuyên suốt năm đoạn: đoạn 1 giới thiệu xích lô (cyclo) trên đường phố Việt Nam và trải nghiệm tham quan chậm rãi của du khách; đoạn 2 kể nguồn gốc từ xe kéo tay (rickshaw) thời Pháp thuộc và sự vất vả của nghề kéo xe; đoạn 3 trình bày sự ra đời của xích lô cuối thập niên 1930 với khung kiểu xe đạp và các ưu điểm vượt trội; đoạn 4 theo dấu thời kỳ xích lô là phương tiện giao thông quan trọng, sự gia tăng tài xế trong thời chiến và đà suy giảm sau năm 1975; đoạn 5 nêu vai trò mới gắn với du lịch, văn hóa và mong muốn duy trì hiện diện của xích lô. Phương án đúng cần bao quát trọn vẹn cả quá trình phát triển ở Việt Nam lẫn vai trò hiện nay, tránh các đáp án thu hẹp vào việc tập lái cho khách du lịch, đảo ngược ưu thế xe kéo hay chỉ nói về xe máy sau chiến tranh.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did some people think rickshaw work was unfair?

options.A: Rickshaws quickly became a popular way for officials to travel
options.B: Drivers lost their jobs when French designs arrived in cities
options.C: Passengers refused to pay for journeys across the countryside
options.D: Drivers had to run on foot while pulling the passengers

questions.explanation: quét từ khóa liên quan đến "rickshaw" và "unfair" ở đoạn 2 để tìm lý do xuất phát từ việc người lái phải chạy bộ trên chân để kéo xe chở khách.

questions.stem: The word "limited" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: delayed
options.B: restricted
options.C: banned completely
options.D: carried

questions.explanation: xét động từ "limited" ở đoạn 4 khi mô tả chính quyền một số nơi kiểm soát/giới hạn hoạt động của xích lô trên các tuyến đường đông đúc (khác với cấm hoàn toàn); ngữ cảnh hướng tới việc bị hạn chế, giới hạn.

questions.stem: The word "They" in paragraph 3 refers to _______.

options.A: French designers
options.B: The first cyclos
options.C: Vietnamese cities
options.D: Rickshaws

questions.explanation: Xác định đại từ nhân xưng số nhiều "They" ở đoạn 3 ("The first cyclos arrived in Vietnam around 1939. They were faster and less tiring than rickshaws..."). Đọc ngược lại câu ngay trước đó để tìm chính xác những chiếc xích lô đầu tiên làm đối tượng tham chiếu, tránh nhầm sang nhà thiết kế Pháp, các thành phố Việt Nam hay xe kéo.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how was the cyclo better than the rickshaw?

options.A: It kept passengers dry with a folding roof in the rainy season
options.B: It could travel between Saigon and Hanoi in a single day
options.C: It was pulled by two drivers who ran together on foot
options.D: It was faster, less tiring, and could carry goods as well

questions.explanation: quét từ khóa so sánh xích lô với xe kéo ("than rickshaws") ở đoạn 3 để xác định các ưu điểm chính được liệt kê cùng nhau (nhanh hơn, ít mệt hơn và chở được cả người lẫn hàng hóa).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT a reason for the decline in cyclos?

options.A: City governments limited cyclos on busy roads
options.B: Tourists stopped visiting the Old Quarter of Hanoi
options.C: Motorbikes became cheaper and faster than cyclos
options.D: Cyclos moved slowly and caused traffic problems

questions.explanation: Đối soát các nguyên nhân khiến số lượng xích lô giảm dần sau năm 1975 được nêu rõ trong đoạn 4 (như xe máy rẻ và nhanh hơn, chính quyền một số nơi hạn chế xích lô trên các tuyến đường đông đúc do chạy chậm và gây vấn đề giao thông). Hãy loại trừ các lý do có xuất hiện trong bài để tìm ra chi tiết không được nhắc đến.

questions.stem: According to the passage, who often became cyclo drivers during the war years?

options.A: Rickshaw drivers who had worked for French officials
options.B: Former soldiers who returned to Saigon after 1975
options.C: City workers who wanted to move to the countryside
options.D: People who had lost their jobs in the countryside

questions.explanation: quét từ khóa về thời kỳ chiến tranh ("during the war years") ở đoạn 4 để tìm nhóm người thường chuyển sang làm nghề đạp xích lô (những người mất việc làm ở nông thôn chuyển ra thành phố).

questions.stem: The word "survive" in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: escape danger
options.B: return quickly
options.C: become popular
options.D: continue to exist

questions.explanation: xét động từ "survive" ở đoạn 5 khi người dân mong xích lô tiếp tục tồn tại giữa nhịp đổi thay nhanh của đô thị; chọn nghĩa tương đương với tiếp tục tồn tại.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from paragraphs 4 and 5 about the cyclo's future?

options.A: It will soon replace motorbikes on the busiest city roads
options.B: It will probably depend more on tourism than on daily transport
options.C: It will disappear from Vietnamese cities within a few years
options.D: It is likely to return as the main form of transport

questions.explanation: Kết hợp thông tin từ đoạn 4 về việc ít người dùng xích lô đi lại hằng ngày hơn trước xe máy với đoạn 5 về sự ưa chuộng của khách du lịch và vai trò dẫn tour/văn hóa. Từ hai đoạn này ghép lại, rút ra kết luận hợp lý về việc tương lai của xích lô nhiều khả năng dựa vào du lịch hơn là giao thông đi lại thường nhật.

questions.stem: What is the writer's attitude toward the cyclo?

options.A: Sad, because tourists now ignore it completely
options.B: Critical, because it causes serious traffic problems in cities
options.C: Neutral, because it has no importance for modern life
options.D: Warm and respectful, seeing it as part of Vietnamese culture Reading

questions.explanation: Quan sát giọng điệu xuyên suốt bài viết từ đoạn 1 đến đoạn 5: người viết mô tả trải nghiệm thư thả, ghi nhận vai trò văn hóa - nghệ thuật và nhắc đến mong muốn giữ gìn xích lô của cư dân. Hãy chọn phương án phản ánh đúng sự ấm áp, trân trọng này, tránh các đáp án buồn bã tuyệt vọng, chỉ trích gay gắt hay thờ ơ.

Đọc ngược lại câu ngay trước đó để tìm chính xác những chiếc xích lô đầu tiên làm đối tượng tham chiếu, tránh nhầm sang nhà thiết kế Pháp, các thành phố Việt Nam hay xe kéo.

parts.title: Behind the Curtain: The Stories of Famous Ballets
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Ask someone to name a ballet and the answer is likely to be Swan Lake or The Nutcracker, works so familiar that it is easy to assume they were instant triumphs. In fact, the histories behind famous ballets are far more uneven, full of **lukewarm** premieres, borrowed stories, and revivals that rescued works their first audiences hardly noticed.

The art form itself took shape in the courts of Renaissance Italy before flourishing in France, where Louis XIV, himself a keen dancer, founded an academy of dance in 1661. French terminology, still used in ballet studios worldwide, dates from that era. Over the following two centuries, ballet moved from courtly spectacle toward storytelling, and by the 1830s and 1840s the Romantic movement had made supernatural tales and fragile heroines its signature subjects.

Giselle, first staged at the Paris Opera in 1841, is the clearest example. Its heroine is a peasant girl who dies of heartbreak after discovering that the man she loves is a nobleman already engaged to someone else. In the second act she joins the Wilis, ghostly spirits of betrayed young women, who force men to dance until they collapse. The story drew on a legend that the poet Heinrich Heine had described, and the ballet's white-clad, otherworldly corps became a **template** that later choreographers copied for generations.

Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake had a rockier start. Premiered at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre in 1877, it was **his** first ballet, and many critics and audiences found the choreography weak and the score unusually demanding for dancers accustomed to lighter music. The work faded from the repertory within a decade. Only after the composer's death in 1893 did it return to prominence, in an 1895 production at St. Petersburg's Mariinsky Theatre staged by Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov, whose choreography for the lakeside scenes remains the core of many versions today.

The Nutcracker, premiered at the Mariinsky in 1892, followed a similar pattern of mixed reception. Adapted from a tale by E. T. A. Hoffmann through a French retelling by Alexandre Dumas, its plot struck some critics as thin, though Tchaikovsky's music, especially the orchestral suite he extracted from it, was praised from the outset. What turned it into a global holiday ritual came much later: in 1954, George Balanchine's production for New York City Ballet proved so popular that companies across the United States began staging their own versions each December.

Behind the scenes, these works owed as much to collaboration as to composition. Marius Petipa, who dominated Russian ballet for decades, typically gave his composers detailed instructions, and Tchaikovsky is reported to have followed them closely when writing The Nutcracker, even down to the number of bars required for each dance. Such tight control may sound restrictive, yet it came at a time when many composers were expected to provide little more than background music, and Tchaikovsky's insistence on treating ballet scores as serious music helped change that expectation.

Together, these stories suggest that a ballet's fame is rarely a measure of its first reception. Public taste, a gifted revival, or simply the habit of an annual tradition can lift a work from obscurity, and the most familiar titles on today's stages are, in a sense, the survivors of repeated second chances.

parts.title: Traffic in Vietnam: Chaos, Cures, and a Comparison with Britain
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: To the visitor, Vietnamese traffic is a spectacle: streams of motorbikes flow around cars, vendors, and pedestrians in a pattern that seems chaotic but works because everyone moves slowly and watches everyone else. Yet the charm of the scene conceals the real costs. In a country where tens of millions of motorbikes are registered, the machine that gave ordinary families mobility has also become the source of some of the nation's most stubborn urban problems.

The statistics are **sobering**. Reports from the authorities have put annual road deaths at roughly ten thousand, a toll that places Vietnam among the more dangerous countries for road users in Asia. Congestion in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City eats into commuters' days, exhaust fumes contribute to air pollution that regularly exceeds recommended limits, and pavements are so often occupied by parked bikes that pedestrians are pushed into the road. Few of these problems are new; what is striking is how long they have been tolerated.

Critics argue that the weakness lies less in ideas than in follow-through. Rules are frequently announced with **fanfare** and then softened or delayed. Hanoi's directive to bar petrol motorbikes from the area inside its first ring road by mid-2026, for instance, was later reshaped into a phased pilot of low-emission zones in selected central wards. Urban metro lines, which could offer a genuine alternative, opened years behind schedule, and until riders have a credible substitute, restrictions risk punishing the very people with the fewest options. Supporters of the authorities reply that change on this scale must be gradual, and that abrupt bans could damage livelihoods, including those of delivery riders and street vendors.

It would be unfair, however, to suggest that nothing has worked. A national requirement for motorbike riders to wear helmets, introduced in 2007, is widely credited with saving many lives, and stricter penalties for drink-driving in recent years appear to have reduced evening fatalities. **These successes** share a feature: they were simple, clearly communicated, and enforced consistently enough that people believed the rules were real.

Britain offers a useful, if imperfect, comparison. Over the past six decades its government has combined legislation with pricing: the breathalyser arrived in 1967, front-seat belts became compulsory in 1983, and in 2003 London introduced a congestion charge that drivers pay to enter the city center. Road deaths have since fallen below two thousand a year, a fraction of Vietnam's toll when population is taken into account. Yet British policy has hardly been free of controversy. The expansion of London's Ultra Low Emission Zone across all boroughs in 2023 provoked fierce protest, and critics at home regularly complain about potholes, delayed rail projects, and costs that rise faster than promised.

What, then, can Vietnam learn? Not that British methods can be copied wholesale; a megacity dependent on cheap motorbikes faces different constraints from a country with an extensive car and rail culture. The lesson is subtler: policies endure when they are phased, explained, and backed by alternatives, and when officials accept short-term unpopularity in exchange for long-term benefit. Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

Phương án đúng cần bao quát trọn vẹn việc vấn đề giao thông của Việt Nam gắn với sự thiếu nhất quán/thực thi chưa trọn vẹn và có thể được cải thiện nhờ chính sách kiên định, tránh các đáp án quy chụp thất bại hoàn toàn, đổ lỗi tuyệt đối cho xe máy hoặc coi giải pháp nước ngoài là bản sao áp dụng máy móc.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R3Q1, R3Q4, R3Q9):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Scanning** (Đọc quét từ khóa đặc hiệu) để đối chiếu thông tin trực tiếp trong từng đoạn được chỉ định.
  - Với **R3Q1**, quét từ khóa liên quan đến kế hoạch hạn chế/cấm xe máy xăng trong vành đai 1 của Hà Nội ở đoạn 3 để xác định hướng điều chỉnh thành thí điểm theo từng giai đoạn của các vùng phát thải thấp (low-emission zones).
  - Với **R3Q4**, quét tên vùng phát thải siêu thấp của London ("Ultra Low Emission Zone") ở đoạn 5 để tìm ý nghĩa minh họa về việc các biện pháp giao thông ở Anh cũng vấp phải sự phản đối mạnh mẽ từ công chúng.

- **Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q8):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Context Clues** (Manh mối ngữ cảnh) kết hợp phân tích cấu trúc câu.
  - Với **R3Q3**, xét tính từ **"sobering"** ở đoạn 2 khi mô tả các con số hoặc thực tế nghiêm trọng khiến người đọc phải nhìn nhận nghiêm túc, tỉnh táo hơn; ngữ cảnh hướng tới sắc thái nghiêm trọng, đáng suy ngẫm.

Từ hai đoạn này ghép lại, rút ra kết luận hợp lý về việc hiệu quả của các hạn chế phụ thuộc vào phương án thay thế khả thi và sự thực thi nhất quán.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Thái độ tác giả (R3Q10):** Quan sát giọng điệu xuyên suốt bài viết khi đánh giá chính sách giao thông của Việt Nam: tác giả ghi nhận những bước đi hoặc kết quả tích cực đạt được nhưng chỉ ra thẳng thắn sự thiếu đồng bộ, đứt gãy trong triển khai và kêu gọi duy trì nhất quán hơn. Hãy chọn phương án phản ánh đúng thái độ phê bình nhưng công bằng này, tránh các đáp án bàng quan, tung hô vượt trội hoặc miệt thị.
Lời khuyên: Hãy xử lý trước nhóm câu hỏi có tọa độ rõ ràng và tập trung vào từ/cụm từ như Quy chiếu (R3Q5) và Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q8). Tiếp theo, dùng kỹ thuật đọc quét để giải quyết nhanh nhóm Chi tiết (R3Q1, R3Q4, R3Q9) và **Loại trừ NOT** (R3Q6). Cuối cùng, khi đã nắm trọn vẹn mạch thông tin và mối liên hệ giữa các đoạn, bạn sẽ dễ dàng chốt đáp án chính xác cho ba câu hỏi tổng hợp gồm **Suy luận** (R3Q7), **Thái độ tác giả** (R3Q10) và **Ý chính toàn** bài (R3Q2).

parts.title: Neptune: The Distant Planet Whose Scientific Stock Is Rising
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For most of human history Neptune was simply unknown. Invisible to the naked eye, it was identified in 1846 not by a lucky glance through a telescope but by mathematics, after astronomers noticed that Uranus was drifting from its predicted path and **inferred** that an unseen body was tugging on it. Urbain Le Verrier in France and John Couch Adams in Britain independently calculated where it should be, and Johann Galle, working in Berlin, found it within about a degree of Le Verrier's prediction.

Neptune's remoteness shapes everything about it. More than thirty times farther from the Sun than Earth, it receives only a sliver of sunlight and takes roughly 165 years to complete a single orbit, so it completed its first full orbit since its discovery only in 2011. Yet its atmosphere is far from quiet. Winds there have been measured at close to two thousand kilometers per hour, among the fastest in the solar system, an observation that puzzles scientists because so little solar energy is available to drive them.

Almost everything detailed that humanity knows of Neptune dates from a single event: the flyby of Voyager 2 in August 1989, the only spacecraft visit the planet has ever received. **[A]** The probe revealed a dark storm system, faint rings, and a magnetic field tilted at a sharp angle and offset from the planet's center. **[B]** Voyager also photographed Triton, Neptune's largest moon, where plumes appeared to rise from the surface. **[C]** Not until a future mission arrives, if one is ever approved, will scientists be able to test the many ideas those few hours of data inspired. **[D]**

Telescopes, however, have begun to fill the gap. In 2025, researchers reported that the James Webb Space Telescope had captured the first clear images of auroras on Neptune, using infrared observations taken in 2023 that revealed a glowing ion in the planet's upper atmosphere. Auroras had already been seen on Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus, so **the** result completed the set among the giant planets. What made the finding intriguing was where the glow appeared: at mid-latitudes rather than clustered around the poles as on Earth, a pattern that scientists link to Neptune's strongly tilted magnetic field.

Neptune's growing prominence owes something to developments far beyond the solar system. Among the thousands of planets discovered around other stars, many of the most common are of similar size to Neptune or somewhat smaller, so understanding Neptune itself matters if astronomers want to interpret those distant worlds. Rarely has a single planet served so conveniently as a local benchmark for an entire class of objects, yet it can fulfill that role only if its composition, interior, and weather are understood far better than they are now.

The case for returning is therefore growing, although no mission to Neptune has yet been approved. Space agencies have studied concepts for orbiters, some of which would also study Triton, and a recent US priority list for planetary science placed a Uranus mission first, leaving Neptune further down the queue. Even a mission launched in the next decade would take years to arrive, which means that today's students may be the first to analyze fresh data from the planet.

Neptune therefore illustrates how a planet can become scientifically fashionable without becoming any closer. Its **allure** lies in what remains unknown: the source of its energy, the nature of its interior, and the reasons its atmosphere behaves so violently so far from the Sun. Only with new data will those questions move from speculation toward answers.

Đọc câu chủ đề và nắm mạch lập luận xuyên suốt toàn bài: đoạn 1 mở đầu bằng việc sao Hải Vương được phát hiện nhờ tính toán thiên văn và xác định vị trí; các đoạn tiếp theo lần lượt trình bày dữ liệu từ chuyến bay ngang qua của Voyager 2 (khí quyển, bão tối, từ trường, vệ tinh Triton), quan sát gần đây bằng kính thiên văn không gian Webb, ý nghĩa của sao Hải Vương đối với việc nghiên cứu ngoại hành tinh kích thước tương tự, cùng những câu hỏi lớn còn bỏ ngỏ và sức hút khoa học của hành tinh này. - **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R4Q1, R4Q7):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Scanning** (Đọc quét từ khóa đặc hiệu) để đối chiếu thông tin trực tiếp trong từng đoạn được chỉ định.
  - Với **R4Q1**, quét từ khóa liên quan đến cách sao Hải Vương được nhận diện/xác định ở đoạn 1 để tìm chuỗi bước: các nhà thiên văn tính toán vị trí từ độ lệch quỹ đạo của sao Thiên Vương, sau đó Galle định vị được hành tinh.
  - Với **R4Q7**, quét từ khóa về các hành tinh quanh các ngôi sao khác (ngoại hành tinh) ở đoạn 5 để tìm lý do sao Hải Vương có giá trị tham chiếu: nhiều ngoại hành tinh phổ biến có kích thước tương đương sao Hải Vương.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q4):** Đối soát các đặc điểm hoặc hiện tượng mà tàu Voyager 2 ghi nhận/chụp ảnh tại hệ sao Hải Vương được nêu trong bài (như bão tối trong khí quyển, từ trường lệch tâm và nghiêng góc lớn, hay các cột phun trào trên bề mặt vệ tinh Triton). Đọc ngược lại các câu trước đó trong đoạn để tìm chính xác kết quả quan sát/phát hiện cực quang bằng kính thiên văn Webb vừa được nhắc đến làm đối tượng tham chiếu, tránh nhầm sang tập hợp các hành tinh khí khổng lồ/băng khổng lồ, cực quang trên sao Thiên Vương hay chuyến bay ngang qua của Voyager 2.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chèn câu vào đoạn văn (R4Q6):** Phân tích nội dung câu cần chèn ("Its orbit runs opposite to the planet's rotation, a clue that Triton was probably captured from the outer solar system rather than formed alongside Neptune.") — câu này đòi hỏi phía trước phải giới thiệu vệ tinh **Triton** ("Its orbit", "Triton") và chuyển động/đặc điểm quỹ đạo của nó để làm căn cứ cho giả thuyết bị bắt giữ từ vùng rìa hệ Mặt Trời. Hãy đối chiếu vị trí xuất hiện của Triton trong đoạn 3 để chọn ô vuông **[A]**, **[B]**, **[C]**, hoặc **[D]** khớp nhất về cả nghĩa lẫn mạch liên kết.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q8):** Kết hợp thông tin từ đoạn 3 về những khám phá nhưng cũng còn nhiều câu hỏi từ lần bay ngang duy nhất của Voyager 2 với đoạn 6 về các bí ẩn cấu trúc bên trong/khí quyển/từ trường chưa thể giải đáp trọn vẹn từ xa. Từ hai đoạn này ghép lại, rút ra kết luận hợp lý về việc các bước tiến lớn trong hiểu biết nhiều khả năng cần một sứ mệnh tàu thăm dò chuyên biệt tới tận nơi.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Thái độ tác giả (R4Q10):** Quan sát giọng điệu xuyên suốt bài viết khi bàn về nghiên cứu sao Hải Vương: tác giả thể hiện sự quan tâm khoa học rõ rệt nhưng giữ mức độ chừng mực, nêu bật cả các phát hiện nổi bật lẫn những câu hỏi lớn còn để ngỏ. Hãy chọn phương án phản ánh đúng sự quan tâm và chừng mực này, tránh các đáp án hoảng hốt, thất vọng phủ nhận hay hoài nghi phóng đại.
Lời khuyên: Hãy xử lý trước nhóm câu hỏi có tọa độ rõ ràng và tập trung vào từ/cụm từ như Quy chiếu (R4Q5) và Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q2, R4Q9). Tiếp theo, dùng kỹ thuật đọc quét để giải quyết nhanh nhóm Chi tiết (R4Q1, R4Q7), Loại trừ NOT (R4Q4) và Chèn câu (R4Q6). Cuối cùng, khi đã nắm trọn vẹn mạch thông tin và mối liên hệ giữa các đoạn, bạn sẽ dễ dàng chốt đáp án chính xác cho các câu hỏi tổng hợp gồm **Suy luận** (R4Q8), **Thái độ tác giả** (R4Q10) và **Tóm** tắt toàn bài (R4Q3).

parts.title: The History of the Coffeehouse
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Coffee is believed to have first been discovered in Ethiopia, where local legend says a goat herder noticed his goats becoming energetic after eating berries from a certain bush. From there, the practice of brewing coffee spread across the Red Sea into Yemen, where people began drinking it regularly by the fifteenth century. As the drink grew popular, small shops selling coffee started to appear, giving people a new place to meet and talk. Traders carried the habit further along established routes, introducing coffee to new regions one city at a time.

These early coffeehouses spread quickly through major cities of the Ottoman world, including Mecca, Cairo, and Istanbul. Unlike taverns, which served alcohol, coffeehouses offered a place where people could gather without the effects of drinking, so conversations tended to stay clearer and often lasted for hours. Customers came to hear music, play games, discuss local news, and sometimes debate religion and politics. Some rulers grew nervous about these gatherings and tried, without much success, to shut coffeehouses down, worried that open discussion might encourage unwanted criticism of their rule.

Coffee eventually reached Europe through trade routes, arriving first in Venice before spreading north to cities such as London and Paris. In London, coffeehouses became known as penny universities, since a customer could pay just one penny for a cup of coffee and spend hours listening to educated discussions on science, business, and current events. Many important institutions, including early insurance companies and stock exchanges, actually began inside these busy, crowded coffeehouses. In Paris, cafes became closely linked with writers and philosophers, who used **them** as informal meeting places to share new ideas, some of which later shaped major political movements.

By the twentieth century, coffee culture had spread across the globe, and coffee itself had become one of the most widely traded goods in the world. Large coffee chains opened in cities everywhere, making the drink more convenient but, according to some critics, less **distinctive** than the coffeehouses of earlier centuries. In response, a newer movement focused on specialty and locally roasted coffee has grown steadily, emphasizing quality and the story behind each cup rather than speed alone. Small independent cafes in many cities now compete directly with these larger chains for **loyal** customers.

Today, cafes serve many different purposes beyond simply selling coffee. Many people use them as informal offices, meeting friends, studying, or working on laptops for hours at a time. Despite all these changes, the basic idea behind the coffeehouse has stayed remarkably consistent since its earliest days: a shared space where people can gather, talk, and exchange ideas over a warm drink. Whatever form the modern cafe takes, this social function appears likely to continue for generations to come.

parts.title: Weaving Silk From Lotus Stems in Hanoi
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Among Vietnam's many traditional crafts, few are as unusual or as labor-intensive as weaving fabric from lotus stems. Unlike ordinary silk, which comes from the cocoons of silkworms, lotus silk is drawn from thin fibers hidden inside the stem of the lotus plant, a flower already deeply associated with Vietnamese culture and Buddhist symbolism. Turning these fragile threads into wearable cloth requires patience that few other textile techniques demand.

The process begins the moment a lotus stem is cut, since the fibers inside begin to dry and lose their usefulness within just a few hours. Artisans must snap each stem carefully, then pull and twist the exposed threads by hand to draw out delicate strands of fiber. These strands are rolled together on a flat surface to form a single continuous thread, a step that demands a steady hand and considerable practice to avoid breaking the fragile material.

The craft owes much of its modern revival to Phan Thi Thuan, a weaver from Phung Xa village on the outskirts of Hanoi, who spent years experimenting with lotus fibers after decades of working with traditional silkworm silk. Her persistence eventually produced a reliable method for turning lotus stems into workable thread, a technical achievement that had **eluded** many earlier attempts by other artisans in the region.

The scale of labor involved is difficult to overstate. Producing just one meter of lotus silk fabric can require several thousand lotus stems, each processed almost entirely by hand within a narrow window of time after harvesting. Because of this intensity, a single skilled weaver can typically complete only a very limited length of fabric per month, which keeps overall production small no matter how much demand might exist. This scarcity, combined with the fabric's soft texture and natural, faintly herbal scent, has helped lotus silk attract attention well beyond Vietnam. Some international fashion houses have expressed interest in the material, drawn partly by its novelty and partly by its environmentally friendly production process, which avoids the synthetic dyes and chemical treatments common in much of the textile industry. Prices for finished lotus silk products remain correspondingly high, reflecting the sheer number of hours embedded in every piece, a cost few casual buyers are willing to cover, though collectors continue to seek **them** out.

Despite this growing recognition, the craft faces real challenges in surviving into the next generation. Very few artisans currently possess the specialized skill needed to extract and weave lotus fiber reliably, and the physically demanding, low-yield nature of the work makes it a difficult sell to younger workers who might otherwise pursue faster-paying trades. Training programs have begun in some villages, though it remains unclear whether enough new weavers will commit to mastering such a **painstaking** craft.

Whether lotus silk weaving expands into a larger, sustainable industry or remains a rare specialty practiced by only a handful of artisans will likely depend on finding buyers willing to pay for its labor rather than its speed of production. For now, the craft persists mainly through the dedication of individuals determined not to let a distinctly Vietnamese tradition disappear.

parts.title: Left-Handedness: Weighing the Pros and Cons
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Roughly one in ten people worldwide is left-handed, a proportion that has stayed remarkably stable across cultures and historical periods studied so far. For centuries, left-handedness carried a social stigma, often linked in folklore and language to clumsiness, dishonesty, or even bad luck. Modern science treats the trait far more neutrally, viewing it as one ordinary outcome of how the brain organizes motor control, rather than as a defect requiring correction.

The biological basis of handedness remains only partly understood, despite decades of scientific attention. Researchers have identified a modest genetic component, since handedness tends to run in families, though no single gene determines it outright. Brain lateralization, the tendency for each hemisphere to specialize in different functions, appears closely tied to hand preference, but scientists still debate exactly how prenatal development settles on one dominant hand rather than the other.

Left-handedness carries certain situational advantages, particularly in combat-style sports such as fencing, boxing, and tennis. Right-handed opponents, who train mostly against other right-handers, often find a left-handed opponent's angles and timing unfamiliar, giving left-handed athletes a disproportionate presence at elite levels of these sports. Some researchers have also proposed that left-handed individuals show slightly greater cognitive flexibility on certain tasks, though this finding remains contested and the effect, if real, appears small. Sports scientists sometimes call this the fighting-left-hander hypothesis.

Everyday life, by contrast, often works against left-handed people, since most common tools and environments were designed with right-handed users in mind. Scissors, school desks, and even some kitchen equipment can feel awkward or genuinely difficult for a left-handed user to operate comfortably. These frictions are minor individually but can accumulate into a persistent, low-level inconvenience that right-handed people rarely have to think about, though many left-handed adults report noticing **it** daily nonetheless.

Older research once suggested more serious risks, including claims that left-handed people had shorter average lifespans and faced higher rates of certain health problems. Much of this research has since been seriously questioned on methodological grounds. A key issue was a cohort effect: many older left-handed adults in these studies had been forcibly switched to right-handed writing as children. This common practice from decades ago likely **confounded** whatever the original data seemed to show.

Social attitudes toward left-handedness have shifted considerably since the mid-twentieth century, and the practice of forcing left-handed children to switch hands has become far less common in most countries. Manufacturers now sell specialized left-handed scissors, desks, and other tools far more widely than before, gradually reducing the everyday friction earlier generations of left-handers simply had to tolerate without complaint. Schools in many countries have also grown noticeably more **accommodating** of left-handed students in recent decades.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that being left-handed is neither a hidden advantage nor a meaningful disadvantage in any general sense. Whatever benefits or drawbacks exist appear to depend heavily on specific context, from the sport being played to the tools available in a given kitchen. Framing handedness as inherently good or bad, the current research suggests, misses just how situational its effects actually are.

parts.title: When Penguins Were Giants
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: The largest living penguin, the emperor penguin, stands at just over a meter tall, a size that already seems impressive to anyone watching one waddle across Antarctic ice. Fossil evidence, however, suggests that penguins were once considerably larger, with some ancient species reaching heights that would have brought them roughly level with an adult human. These giant penguins vanished long before humans existed, known to us only through fragments of bone recovered from ancient coastal rock.

Among the most striking fossil finds is Kumimanu biceae, a species described from bones discovered in New Zealand and estimated to have lived between fifty-five and sixty million years ago. Researchers calculated that this penguin likely stood around one and a half meters tall and weighed close to eighty kilograms, **dwarfing** any penguin alive today. Several other giant species have since been identified from similar fossil beds, suggesting that unusually large penguins were not a single evolutionary fluke but a recurring pattern in early penguin history.

Estimating the size of an animal known only from scattered bones is inherently uncertain work. Paleontologists typically rely on the dimensions of preserved limb bones, comparing them against scaling relationships observed in living penguins, to infer overall body size and mass. Because complete skeletons are rare, these estimates carry meaningful margins of error, and researchers are generally careful to describe such figures as best approximations rather than settled fact. A single new, more complete fossil can sometimes shift **it** considerably.

Why penguins grew so large in this early period remains a matter of ongoing debate, though one hypothesis has attracted particular attention. Shortly after the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs, marine ecosystems lacked many of the large predators, such as seals and toothed whales, that dominate today's oceans. With fewer competitors and predators pursuing similar prey in coastal waters, some researchers argue, penguins may have been free to evolve toward considerably larger body sizes than would otherwise have been sustainable.

That relatively open ecological niche did not last indefinitely. As millions of years passed, marine mammals diversified substantially, and seals and early whales began competing directly with penguins for fish and squid in the same coastal waters. Many researchers suspect that this rising competition, combined with new predation pressure, gradually favored smaller, more maneuverable penguins over their giant ancestors. Pinning down the exact pace and mechanism of this shift, however, remains genuinely difficult using fossils alone.

Other explanations have also been proposed alongside the competition hypothesis, and the field has not settled on a single, agreed-upon account. Some researchers point to possible thermoregulation advantages tied to large body size in cold Southern Ocean waters. Others emphasize physical constraints on diving depth and swimming efficiency that may have limited how large a penguin could practically become while remaining an effective underwater hunter. Most specialists now treat these explanations as complementary rather than competing, since several pressures likely acted together rather than in isolation.

The **fragmentary** fossil record of giant penguins continues to be reshaped by new discoveries that refine scientists' understanding of the timeline involved. Each newly described species adds another data point to a picture that is still, by most paleontologists' own admission, more suggestive than definitive. What does seem clear is that today's comparatively modest penguins represent only one chapter in a much longer, and considerably larger-scaled, evolutionary story that fossil hunters are still piecing together.

parts.title: Myanmar: A General Introduction
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Myanmar is a large country in Southeast Asia, bordered by China, India, Thailand, Laos, and Bangladesh. With a population of more than fifty million people, it is one of the biggest countries in the region by both land area and population. Its capital city is Naypyidaw, though the largest and most famous city is Yangon, once the country's capital and still its main center for business and culture. Many visitors are surprised to learn how varied the country's landscape is, from mountains in the north to a long coastline in the south. The country is also crossed by several major rivers that support farming and transportation across many regions.

For much of the twentieth century, Myanmar was known internationally as Burma, and the country experienced decades of military rule that limited contact with the outside world. In recent years, Myanmar has gone through significant political change, though the situation remains complicated and still affects daily life for many citizens. Because of this history, some older maps and books still use the name Burma instead of Myanmar. Understanding this background helps explain why the country is less familiar to many travelers than some of its neighbors.

Buddhism plays a central role in Myanmar's culture, and most of the population follows this religion closely. Golden pagodas can be found in almost every town, and the most famous of these, the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon, attracts both worshippers and tourists from around the world. Traditional festivals connected to the Buddhist calendar are celebrated throughout the year with music, food, and colorful processions. Local cuisine blends influences from neighboring China, India, and Thailand, resulting in dishes that use rice, fish, and a wide range of spices. Tea leaf salad, a dish unique to the region, remains one of the most popular foods among both locals and visitors.

Agriculture remains central to Myanmar's economy, with rice as the most important crop grown across the **fertile** plains near the Irrawaddy River. The country is also known for natural resources such as jade, teak wood, and natural gas, which are exported to neighboring countries, since demand for **them** continues to grow steadily. Despite these resources, Myanmar remains one of the less developed economies in Southeast Asia, and many rural communities still lack reliable access to electricity and modern transportation. Economic growth has been **uneven**, with cities developing far faster than most parts of the countryside in recent decades.

In recent years, growing numbers of travelers have become interested in visiting Myanmar to see its temples, rivers, and traditional villages. The ancient city of Bagan, home to thousands of historic pagodas spread across a wide plain, has become especially popular among tourists. However, limited infrastructure and ongoing political instability continue to make travel and investment more difficult than in some neighboring countries. Many observers believe that Myanmar's long-term development will depend heavily on how these underlying challenges are eventually addressed.

parts.title: Vietnamese Women Today: What Has Changed
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For much of the twentieth century, the expected role of a Vietnamese woman centered heavily on the household: raising children, managing domestic finances, and deferring to the judgment of a husband or father figure. That expectation drew on centuries of Confucian influence, which placed a woman's primary value in her contribution to family harmony rather than to public or professional life. Over the past few decades, however, that picture has shifted substantially, even if the shift remains far from complete.

Education has been one of the clearest engines of this change. Women now make up roughly half of university students nationwide, a figure that would have seemed unlikely two generations ago. In some fields, including medicine and business administration, female enrollment has begun to match or exceed that of men. This educational shift has, in turn, reshaped expectations about what a young woman's life might look like after graduation, opening doors largely closed to her grandmother's generation.

Vietnam has long had comparatively high female labor force participation by regional standards, but the nature of that participation has been changing. Rather than concentrating in agriculture or informal trade, as earlier generations often did, growing numbers of women now work in management, technology, and entrepreneurship. Female-led startups have become increasingly visible in cities such as Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, and business associations specifically supporting women entrepreneurs have multiplied over the past decade.

Marriage and family patterns have shifted alongside these economic changes. The average age at which women marry has risen steadily, and many now spend years building a career or completing further education before starting a family, a sequence unusual a generation ago. Family size has also declined, partly reflecting greater autonomy over reproductive decisions and partly reflecting the practical demands of balancing paid work with raising children. Many young couples now discuss these decisions together long before marriage, a shift from earlier generations who rarely questioned **them**.

Despite this progress, significant inequalities persist beneath the surface of these gains. Surveys consistently find that employed women still perform a disproportionate share of housework and childcare, a pattern researchers describe as a double burden. Paid employment, in other words, has rarely been matched by a corresponding redistribution of domestic responsibility. Women also remain underrepresented in the most senior levels of corporate and political leadership, even in sectors where they form the majority of the workforce.

These changes, moreover, have not spread evenly across the country. Urban women, especially in major cities, tend to experience far more dramatic shifts in education, career opportunity, and social expectation than their rural counterparts, where traditional family structures often remain more firmly **entrenched**. This urban-rural divide means that any single description of the modern Vietnamese woman risks **flattening** what is, in practice, a wide range of overlapping and sometimes contradictory experiences.

Taken together, the trajectory is unmistakably one of expanding opportunity, even as older expectations continue to shape daily life in less visible ways. Whether the coming decades bring a fuller redistribution of domestic responsibility, or simply a wider set of demands placed on women who now juggle both roles, will likely depend on shifting cultural attitudes as much as on continued economic progress.

parts.title: AI Assistants, Information Search, and Travel Booking
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For most of the internet era, finding information and booking a trip involved two separate skills: typing the right keywords into a search engine, then navigating a maze of airline and hotel websites to compare prices. Conversational AI assistants are now collapsing that distinction, offering to search, compare, and in some cases complete a booking within a single exchange. What once required a dozen browser tabs increasingly happens inside one conversation.

Underlying most of these assistants is a technique often called retrieval-augmented generation, in which a language model pulls relevant documents or listings from an external source before composing its answer, rather than relying solely on patterns memorized during training. This matters because a model answering purely from memory can confidently state prices, schedules, or availability that are simply out of date. **Grounding** responses in freshly retrieved data is meant to reduce that risk, though it does not eliminate it entirely.

In travel specifically, some assistants have moved beyond merely summarizing options to actually taking action: filling out booking forms, comparing fares across airlines, and completing a purchase once a traveler confirms the details. This shift from answering questions to executing tasks represents a meaningful expansion of what these systems are trusted to do, since a factual error in a summary is inconvenient, while an error during an actual purchase carries real financial consequences.

Proponents argue that this convenience saves considerable time, particularly for travelers juggling multiple constraints such as budget, dates, and layover preferences that are tedious to specify repeatedly across different websites, a burden AI assistants aim to lift from **them**. Some early user studies suggest that people do report saving time compared with manual searching, although the samples in these studies remain small and the tasks tested are not always representative of real booking complexity.

Critics raise a different set of concerns. Because language models can produce fluent, confident text even when incorrect, a travel assistant might describe a nonexistent flight route or misstate a refund policy with no obvious sign that anything is wrong. When such a system is also authorized to complete purchases, the consequences of an undetected error shift from mild embarrassment to a financial dispute, raising questions about who bears responsibility when an AI-initiated booking goes wrong.

These developments are also reshaping the businesses that traditionally sat between travelers and their trips. Online travel agencies and search engines have long earned revenue through advertising and referral fees tied to how results are displayed, a model that assumes a human is scanning a results page. An AI assistant that quietly selects one option on a traveler's behalf disrupts that arrangement, and several companies in the sector are still working out how, or whether, to adapt their revenue models.

None of this suggests that AI travel assistants are simply better or worse than the tools they are replacing; the picture is more mixed than either enthusiasm or alarm would suggest. What seems clearer is that trust in these systems will likely need to be earned **incrementally**, through transparent sourcing and clear accountability when something goes wrong, rather than assumed simply because the underlying technology is impressive.

parts.title: Do Mice Keep Making Eggs? A Contested Finding in Reproductive Biology
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For decades, reproductive biology rested on a tidy assumption: female mammals are born with a fixed, non-renewable supply of egg cells, one that can only shrink, never grow, across a lifetime. In humans, this framework fits the evidence well and helps explain why fertility declines sharply with age as the finite reserve is gradually used up. The assumption seemed settled enough that few researchers thought to question it directly in other species, let alone attempt to overturn it.

That settled picture began to **wobble** in the early 2000s, when a research team led by the biologist Jonathan Tilly reported evidence that adult mouse ovaries contained germline stem cells capable of generating new egg cells well into adulthood. If correct, this would mean that at least some mammals do not simply deplete a fixed store of eggs but can, under certain conditions, keep producing more, a possibility the earlier dogma had ruled out almost by definition. The claim, unsurprisingly, did not sit quietly within the field.

The implications, had the finding held up cleanly, would have been considerable. A renewable egg supply might eventually inform new approaches to treating age-related infertility, or even suggest that reproductive aging is more biologically flexible than long assumed. It is little surprise that the original papers drew intense attention, both from specialists eager to test the claim and from a wider public hungry for any hint that fertility decline might someday be reversible. Some early commentary even speculated about implications for human fertility treatment, well ahead of any confirming evidence.

That attention, however, was quickly matched by skepticism. Several independent laboratories attempted to replicate the original findings and reported difficulty confirming that the proposed stem cells behaved as claimed, or that they meaningfully contributed new eggs rather than merely resembling egg precursors in appearance. Debate over methodology, cell markers, and interpretation continued for years, and the reproductive biology community remained visibly split on how much weight the original claims deserved. Some researchers came to view the entire concept with active suspicion.

More recent studies, employing more rigorous lineage-tracing techniques that genetically mark cells and track their descendants over time, have offered partial and heavily qualified support for limited postnatal egg formation in mice under specific experimental conditions. This is a considerably narrower claim than the original, striking suggestion of an essentially unlimited or continuously renewing supply. Most researchers now describe the phenomenon, if it exists at all, as modest and tightly conditional rather than transformative.

Whether any of this translates to humans remains, at best, an open question rather than an established fact. Mice and humans differ substantially in reproductive lifespan and ovarian structure, and in the pace at which egg reserves are used, so a mechanism documented cautiously in mice cannot simply be assumed to operate the same way in women. Researchers who study this question tend to describe extrapolation to humans as premature rather than merely uncertain, a distinction that matters considerably in how the findings are communicated publicly.

None of this scientific caution has entirely stopped commercial interest from moving faster than the evidence. Some fertility clinics have marketed procedures described as ovarian stem-cell therapy or egg rejuvenation, implying a level of scientific confidence that the underlying research does not yet support. Many reproductive biologists have publicly criticized this gap between marketing claims and unsettled science, arguing that hopeful patients deserve a clearer picture of how tentative the underlying findings still are.

- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q6):** Tổng hợp danh sách các lý do cần cẩn trọng khi áp dụng kết quả từ chuột sang người ở các đoạn giữa (khác biệt về vòng đời sinh sản, cấu trúc buồng trứng, tốc độ tiêu thụ dự trữ), sau đó đối soát 4 phương án để chọn nhận định không được đề cập.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q7):** Kết hợp các lập luận ở các đoạn 5 và 6 về việc nếu hiện tượng sản xuất trứng liên tục ở chuột có thật thì nó cũng chỉ ở mức độ hạn chế/nhỏ chứ không mang tính đột phá lớn như kỳ vọng ban đầu.

parts.title: Why Failure Can Fuel Motivation
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Most people see failure as something to avoid, a clear sign that a plan has gone wrong. Yet across sports, business, and education, many psychologists argue that setbacks often push people to work harder rather than quietly give up, because the disappointment itself creates a strong desire to fix whatever went wrong. This kind of response is not automatic for everyone. For many, though, failure becomes a starting point rather than a final ending, and understanding why this happens can help students, workers, and athletes turn frustrating moments into genuinely useful lessons.

Consider a young runner who fails to qualify for a regional competition after months of steady training. Instead of quitting the sport, she studies her race times closely and notices that her final lap is consistently the slowest part of every race she runs. She begins ending each practice with a short, demanding sprint, deliberately training the exact weakness her failure had revealed. Within a few months her overall time improves noticeably. Her coach later remarks that the missed qualification taught her more than any earlier victory had, because it pointed directly to one fixable problem rather than a vague sense of not being good enough.

Researchers who study motivation say failure works because it gives clear, specific feedback. Winning a race or acing a test mainly confirms that current habits are working, so there is little obvious reason to change anything at all. Losing, on the other hand, forces a person to ask exactly what went wrong, and that question can **sharpen** effort in ways vague encouragement simply cannot match. Some experts describe this shift as turning a broad goal, such as 'get better,' into a narrow, specific one, such as 'improve my final lap by three seconds.'

Failure does not motivate everyone in the same way, however. If a person interprets a setback as proof that they simply lack talent, that same experience can lead to giving up rather than trying again. Supportive teachers, coaches, and parents often shape which of these two responses a student develops, since without steady guidance many young people never learn to reinterpret a setback as useful information. When mistakes are treated as private embarrassments to hide, students tend to avoid future risks, but when adults discuss **them** openly and calmly, students grow far more willing to attempt difficult tasks again.

Because of this, some schools and companies have begun **redesigning** how they respond to failure. Instead of only rewarding final results, several workplaces now recognize employees who took a reasonable risk and learned something valuable from an unsuccessful project. Teachers in a handful of schools ask students to write short reflections on what a wrong answer revealed about their own thinking. These small changes will not turn every failure into progress, but they create the kind of environment in which setbacks are far more likely to become genuinely useful.

parts.title: Firstborns and Later-Borns: Testing an Old Idea
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For more than a century, popular wisdom has insisted that birth order quietly shapes character: firstborns supposedly grow into cautious, responsible leaders, while younger siblings become the rebellious, creative risk-takers of the family. This idea shows up constantly in parenting advice and casual conversation, treated almost as settled fact rather than as a hypothesis. Only in recent decades, however, has the claim been tested with large, carefully controlled studies that could confirm or dismantle it.

The theory traces back largely to Alfred Adler, an early twentieth-century psychologist who argued that a child's position among siblings creates a distinct psychological environment. According to Adler, firstborns briefly enjoy undivided parental attention before being 'dethroned' by a younger sibling, an experience he believed could produce either heightened responsibility or lasting insecurity. Later-born children never experience this loss of exclusive attention, and Adler suggested this made them more inclined to seek **novelty** and recognition.

When researchers finally gathered data from tens of thousands of families rather than small convenience samples, the picture that emerged was far less tidy than Adler's framework implied. A widely cited 2015 analysis found a real but exceptionally small difference in IQ favoring firstborns. Yet the same analysis found almost no reliable birth-order effect on personality traits such as extraversion once family size and social background were taken into account. In other words, whatever influence birth order has appears far narrower than popular stereotypes suggest.

One explanation for the modest IQ difference draws on what psychologists call resource dilution: parents generally have more time and attention to give a single child than they later have to divide among several. A firstborn, for a period, effectively receives an only child's share of parental conversation before that attention must be split. Because early verbal interaction is closely tied to later vocabulary scores, even a small early advantage can persist, faintly, into adulthood.

Family size complicates this picture, since it is tangled up with birth order in ways that are easy to overlook. Families with many children tend, on average, to have different resources than smaller families. Simply comparing firstborns to later-borns across a population therefore risks confusing the effect of birth order with the effect of household size. Researchers who fail to separate these two variables risk attributing to birth order what is really a difference in family circumstances.

To address this problem, more rigorous studies now compare siblings within the very same family rather than firstborns from one household against later-borns from another. This within-family approach removes shared factors like household income, since siblings raised in one home share both. What these studies repeatedly show is that siblings often differ substantially in personality, but that birth order itself explains only a **sliver** of that difference. Far more of **it** comes from each child's own friendships and experiences, factors psychologists group under the label 'non-shared environment.'

None of this means birth order is entirely meaningless, since the small, well-documented IQ effect does appear real. It does suggest, though, that the sweeping personality claims dominating popular culture rest on far shakier evidence than their confidence implies. A younger sibling's future personality, it turns out, is shaped far more by individual experience than by a fixed place in the family lineup.
