parts.title: The Economics and Engineering of Solar Power
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Barely fifteen years ago, solar power was widely dismissed as a marginal technology, too costly and unreliable to matter beyond niche applications such as remote sensors. That dismissal now looks badly outdated. In many regions, newly built solar installations already generate electricity more cheaply than newly built coal or gas plants, a reversal few analysts predicted a decade ago. What changed was not a single breakthrough but a steady accumulation of manufacturing and engineering improvements.

Much of the price collapse traces to what economists call a learning curve: for every doubling of cumulative panel production, manufacturing costs have tended to fall by a fairly consistent percentage. This pattern was first documented in industries as different as aircraft assembly and semiconductors. Larger factories, more automated production lines, and steady gains in silicon efficiency all fed into this curve simultaneously, without any single company or government engineering the outcome deliberately.

Falling costs alone, however, have not solved solar power's central technical problem. The sun does not shine on demand, and electricity, unlike most commodities, must generally be consumed at nearly the same instant it is produced. Grid operators in regions with heavy solar adoption have grown familiar with what is informally called the duck curve, in which demand stays roughly stable through the day while solar output surges at midday. It then plunges toward evening, precisely when household electricity use rises sharply, and meeting that steep ramp with other sources has proven disruptive to grid planning.

Battery storage is often presented as the obvious fix, and its costs have fallen almost as dramatically as solar panels themselves. Yet deploying batteries at a scale large enough to smooth an entire regional grid remains slower and more capital-intensive than installing panels alone. Some utilities have turned instead to demand response programs, which pay customers to shift electricity use away from peak hours, or to older technologies such as pumped hydro storage.

Critics of rapid solar expansion raise concerns that go beyond intermittency. Mining the lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth elements used in panels and batteries carries its own environmental costs, and large solar farms can require substantial land, occasionally displacing agricultural use or natural habitat. Some economists further argue that government subsidies have **distorted** investment decisions, channeling capital toward projects that would not be competitive on cost alone without public support, though supporters counter that fossil fuels long received comparable subsidies with far less scrutiny.

Despite these unresolved debates, investment in solar generation has continued to climb year after year, driven partly by climate policy targets and partly by the economics described earlier. Financial analysts increasingly treat intermittency not as a fatal flaw but as an engineering challenge to be solved alongside falling storage costs and more flexible demand. Whether that optimism proves justified will depend less on the panels themselves than on the **unglamorous** infrastructure built to support them.

Solar power, in short, has already won the argument over cost, but not yet the argument over reliability at full grid scale. Treating **it** as a simple substitute for fossil fuel plants misunderstands the transition underway. A more accurate picture presents solar as one component within a broader system, whose ultimate success depends on parallel progress in storage, transmission, and the flexibility of electricity demand itself.

parts.title: Efficiency, the Rebound Effect, and the Limits of Green Technology
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: It seems intuitively obvious that making something more efficient should reduce its environmental footprint: a car that burns less fuel per mile, a bulb that uses less electricity per lumen, ought straightforwardly to lower total energy consumption. This assumption quietly underpins much environmental policy, from fuel-economy standards to appliance labeling schemes. Rarely questioned in public debate, it turns out to rest on shakier ground than most policymakers acknowledge.

Economists have in fact been skeptical of this assumption for well over a century. In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that Britain's coal consumption rose, rather than fell, after steam engines became dramatically more fuel-efficient, since cheaper operation made coal-powered machinery viable for a far wider range of uses. What later became known as the rebound effect suggests that efficiency gains do not always translate into proportional reductions in total resource use, because they simultaneously make consumption cheaper and therefore more attractive.

Contemporary research paints a genuinely mixed picture rather than confirming Jevons at every turn. Some sectors, such as residential heating in wealthy countries, show only modest rebound: households that upgrade insulation tend to save a meaningful share of the energy that improved efficiency would predict. Other sectors show something closer to what researchers term backfire, in which efficiency gains are more than fully offset by increased use, leaving total consumption higher than before the improvement. Which pattern applies in a given case appears to depend heavily on how price-sensitive that particular form of consumption is.

Two distinct mechanisms are usually distinguished within this broader phenomenon. Direct rebound occurs when a good becomes cheaper to use and people simply use more of it, driving a fuel-efficient car further, for instance, precisely because each mile now costs less. Indirect rebound is subtler: money saved through efficiency in one domain often gets **redirected** toward other, sometimes equally resource-intensive, purchases elsewhere, so that overall environmental savings may not materialize even where direct use does not increase. Isolating this indirect channel empirically remains notoriously difficult.

None of this necessarily implies that efficiency standards are pointless, though some commentators have drawn precisely that conclusion. What the evidence more cautiously suggests is that efficiency alone, unaccompanied by mechanisms that keep the price of resource use from falling, may fail to deliver the reductions its advocates expect. Many economists therefore argue that efficiency regulation works best paired with a price signal, such as a carbon tax, that prevents savings from simply being spent on additional consumption.

Critics of rebound-effect skepticism push back on several fronts. They argue the effect has often been overstated in wealthy economies where demand for basic energy services is largely **saturated**, so that further efficiency gains genuinely do reduce consumption rather than unlocking new demand. The same critics tend to concede, however, that rebound may matter considerably more in rapidly developing economies, where rising incomes and previously unmet demand leave far more room for cheaper energy to unlock consumption that would not otherwise have occurred.

Read carefully, the rebound literature does not argue that efficiency improvements are worthless, nor does it hand critics of environmental policy an easy dismissal of such measures. **It** argues something narrower and more demanding: that efficiency should be treated as a necessary but not sufficient condition for reducing environmental harm, one whose benefits depend on the economic context surrounding it rather than on the technology alone.

parts.title: Life on a Modern Pig Farm
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Pig farming has been part of rural economies for thousands of years, and today it remains one of the most widespread forms of livestock production across the world. In many countries, small family-run farms still raise a handful of pigs for local markets, while large commercial operations manage thousands of animals under a single roof. Vietnam, in particular, has a long tradition of pig raising, with the animal appearing frequently in folk stories and traditional festivals. Modern farms, however, look very different from the backyard pens of the past, relying instead on carefully planned systems that combine science with everyday practical knowledge.

Feeding is one of the most important daily tasks on any pig farm, because the amount and type of food a pig eats directly affects both its health and the quality of the meat it eventually produces. Young piglets typically drink their mother's milk for several weeks before gradually being introduced to a mixture of grains, soybean meal, and vitamins. As the pigs grow larger, farmers adjust the feed to include more energy-rich ingredients such as corn, which helps the animals gain weight steadily rather than too quickly. Clean water must always be available, since pigs can become dehydrated and stressed surprisingly fast in hot weather. Housing also matters a great deal; pens that are too crowded tend to increase fighting among the animals and make it easier for illnesses to spread. Farmers often keep piglets separate from older pigs during the first few weeks, since housing **them** together can lead to injuries from more aggressive animals.

Because pigs are raised so closely together, disease control is treated as a serious and ongoing responsibility rather than an occasional task. Veterinarians recommend a regular schedule of vaccinations to protect against common illnesses, and many farms now keep detailed health records for every animal. When an outbreak such as African swine fever does occur, it can spread with alarming speed and force farmers to cull entire herds within days, wiping out years of careful breeding work. For this reason, most modern farms restrict outside visitors, disinfect vehicles before they enter the property, and separate newly arrived animals from the rest of the herd for a period of observation.

Pork remains one of the most consumed meats globally, and the industry that supplies it generates substantial income for farmers, feed suppliers, and exporters alike. Prices, though, can swing sharply within a single year, since they depend on factors ranging from grain costs to sudden shifts in consumer demand. A farmer who expands too quickly during a period of high prices may find, only months later, that falling prices have made the investment far riskier than it first appeared. Some governments respond to these swings by offering subsidies or temporary price supports, hoping to keep smaller farms from being pushed out of the market entirely.

Large-scale pig farming, while economically important, also raises environmental concerns that communities near major farms are increasingly **vocal** about. Waste from thousands of animals must be collected, treated, and often converted into fertilizer, a process that, if managed poorly, can pollute nearby rivers and contaminate groundwater. Newer farms are experimenting with biogas systems that turn manure into usable energy, offering a partial solution to both waste disposal and rising electricity costs. Whether such technologies become standard practice across the industry, or remain limited to a handful of well-funded operations, will likely shape how sustainably pig farming can continue to expand in the coming decades.

parts.title: Advertising the Magic Worldwide: Disney's Global Park Campaigns
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: When the Walt Disney Company promotes its theme parks abroad, it faces a challenge that few advertisers encounter on the same scale: convincing audiences on nearly every continent that a single brand identity can feel both universally magical and personally relevant. Campaigns for parks in Shanghai, Paris, Tokyo, and Orlando share a recognizable visual language, yet subtle differences in tone, humor, and imagery reveal how deeply each market has been studied before a single advertisement airs. This balancing act, more than any individual slogan, may explain why Disney's advertising has become a frequent case study in international marketing courses.

Rather than simply translating English-language advertisements into other languages, Disney's marketing teams typically rebuild campaigns around local storytelling traditions, holidays, and family customs. In China, for instance, promotional material for Shanghai Disneyland has leaned heavily on themes of multigenerational family togetherness, a value that **resonates** strongly during major national holidays. European campaigns, by contrast, tend to emphasize fantasy and imagination somewhat more than family duty, though the difference is one of degree rather than a strict rule. Such choices are rarely accidental; they emerge from extensive market research that attempts to predict, however imperfectly, what will move a particular audience to book a trip.

Over the past decade, television commercials have gradually given up ground to digital platforms, where short videos, interactive filters, and influencer partnerships now carry much of the promotional weight. A single well-placed video featuring a popular local celebrity visiting a park can generate more engagement, at a fraction of the cost, than a traditional prime-time advertisement ever could. This shift has not eliminated large-scale advertising, however; major openings and anniversaries still receive substantial television and outdoor campaigns, suggesting that digital and traditional media now function less as rivals than as complementary tools aimed at different stages of a potential visitor's decision-making process.

Tourism officials in host cities often argue that a new Disney park delivers economic benefits far beyond ticket sales, and the surrounding evidence, while not conclusive on every point, tends to support at least part of that claim. Hotels, restaurants, and transportation services near Shanghai Disneyland, for example, reported measurable increases in business shortly after the park opened, even among visitors who never entered the gates themselves. Critics counter that such regional advertising campaigns sometimes overstate long-term benefits, since initial surges in visitor spending do not always translate into permanent local employment once the novelty of an opening fades.

Determining exactly how much any single advertisement contributes to eventual ticket sales remains **notoriously** difficult, since a visitor's decision to book a trip may be shaped by years of accumulated brand impressions rather than one recent campaign. Marketing researchers therefore rely on indirect measures, such as website traffic spikes following an ad's release or shifts in search-engine interest for a particular park, to estimate impact rather than to prove it outright. These indirect measures suggest a correlation between campaign timing and booking activity, though **they** cannot fully rule out other explanations, such as seasonal travel patterns that would have driven bookings regardless of any advertising at all.

Not every campaign succeeds, and Disney's advertising history includes several notable missteps, particularly when messaging designed for one cultural context was applied too directly in another without sufficient adjustment. Such failures have pushed the company toward deeper collaboration with regional marketing agencies rather than relying solely on directives issued from a central office. Looking ahead, industry observers expect that artificial intelligence tools, which can rapidly generate and test dozens of localized ad variations, will further blur the line between global brand consistency and hyper-local advertising, even as questions remain about how such tools might affect the distinctive human storytelling that has long defined Disney's marketing.

options.B: Disney's park advertising focuses only on entertainment value, not economic impact
options.C: Local advertising agencies alone determine Disney's global marketing strategy
options.D: Disney relies mainly on television advertising to promote all its parks

parts.title: "Fish Milk": An Unusual Parallel in Nature
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Although the word 'milk' evokes images of mammals such as cows or goats, several species of fish have evolved a strikingly similar strategy for feeding their young. Discus fish, a freshwater species popular among aquarium keepers, secrete a thick, nutrient-dense mucus from specialized glands on their skin, which their offspring graze on directly during the first weeks of life. Because this substance performs many of the same biological functions as mammalian milk — delivering concentrated nutrition, antibodies, and hormones to rapidly growing young — some biologists have begun referring to it informally as 'fish milk,' though the term remains a loose analogy rather than a precise scientific classification.

Laboratory analysis of discus mucus has revealed a composition that shifts noticeably as the fry mature, a pattern that mirrors, at least in broad outline, how mammalian milk changes to match an infant's developmental stage. Early secretions tend to be richer in certain proteins and immune-related compounds, whereas later secretions gradually shift toward a composition better suited to fry that have already begun supplementing their diet with other food sources. Researchers caution, however, that drawing too close a parallel with mammalian lactation risks **obscuring** important differences, since the underlying glandular structures and hormonal triggers evolved entirely independently.

Discus fish are not alone in this behavior; certain skates and at least one species of shark have been documented producing comparable secretions, though the evidence for these species remains considerably thinner than for discus fish, resting largely on isolated field observations rather than controlled laboratory study. Some researchers suspect that similar mechanisms may be more widespread among fish than currently documented, largely because such behavior is difficult to observe in wild populations and is easy to overlook in commercial farms that do not routinely monitor for **it**.

This biological curiosity has attracted attention well beyond academic ichthyology, largely because it intersects with two pressing practical concerns: the difficulty of rearing certain fish species in captivity, and the search for alternative protein sources that place less strain on land and water resources than conventional dairy farming. Aquaculture operations that raise discus fish commercially have long struggled to replicate natural rearing conditions, since separating fry from parents too early, before the natural mucus-feeding period ends, tends to reduce survival rates and stunt growth even when artificial feed is nutritionally complete on paper.

A handful of food-science laboratories have begun exploring whether the nutritional profile of fish-derived secretions could inform the design of novel protein supplements, though this line of research remains at an early, largely exploratory stage rather than anything approaching commercial application. Proponents argue that if a stable, scalable extraction method could be developed, such products might offer an unusually nutrient-dense supplement with a considerably smaller environmental footprint than dairy, since fish generally convert feed into biomass more efficiently than cattle do.

Such optimism, however, invites considerable skepticism from within the scientific community itself. The quantities of mucus a single discus fish produces are **minuscule** compared to the volumes required for even modest commercial food production, and no researcher has yet proposed a method for scaling extraction without harming the animals or fundamentally altering their natural rearing behavior. Whether 'fish milk' ultimately becomes a meaningful contributor to alternative protein markets, or remains a biological footnote of interest mainly to aquarium hobbyists and evolutionary biologists, will depend on breakthroughs that, at present, exist only as speculative possibilities rather than active research programs.

  - Với **R3Q2**, quét từ khóa "shifts" hoặc "composition" ở đoạn 2 để kiểm tra sự biến đổi của dịch tiết theo độ tuổi cá con (chuyển từ các hợp chất miễn dịch ban đầu sang dạng phù hợp cho cá lớn hơn).
  - Với **R3Q4**, quét từ khóa "skates" hoặc "sharks" ở đoạn 3 để xác định căn cứ bằng chứng (chủ yếu dựa vào quan sát thực địa nhỏ lẻ thay vì nghiên cứu phòng thí nghiệm).
  - Với **R3Q8**, quét cụm từ "separating fry from parents too early" ở đoạn 4 để tìm nguyên nhân gây khó khăn cho nuôi trồng thương mại (làm giảm tỷ lệ sống và cản trở sự phát triển của cá).
- **Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q9):** Áp dụng kỹ thuật **Context Clues** (Manh mối ngữ cảnh):
  - Với **R3Q3**, đọc ngữ cảnh đoạn 2 mô tả việc ví von quá mức có nguy cơ che giấu/làm mờ đi (**"obscuring"**) những điểm khác biệt quan trọng để tìm từ đồng nghĩa (concealing).
  - Với **R3Q9**, xét ngữ cảnh đoạn 6 nhấn mạnh lượng dịch tiết cực kỳ nhỏ/ít ỏi (**"minuscule"**) của một con cá đĩa so với quy mô sản xuất thương mại để chọn từ đồng nghĩa thích hợp (tiny).
- **Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R3Q5):** Đọc ngược lại câu trước ở đoạn 3 để xác định danh từ chỉ hành vi/hiện tượng (như việc tiết dịch nuôi con - such behavior) mà các trang trại thương mại dễ dàng bỏ qua do không theo dõi thường xuyên.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R3Q6):** Tổng hợp các lý do đề cập ở đoạn 4 khiến hiện tượng này thu hút sự chú ý (khó khăn nuôi nhốt, tìm nguồn protein ít tiêu tốn tài nguyên), đối soát với các phương án để chọn chi tiết không được nhắc đến.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R3Q7):** Kết hợp thông tin ở đoạn 5 và đoạn 6 về các rào cản quy mô thương mại chưa được giải quyết để suy luận rằng sự thành công trong tương lai hoàn toàn phụ thuộc vào những đột phá hiện chưa xuất hiện.

  - Với **R3Q10**, nhận diện giọng văn của tác giả khi vừa tò mò tìm hiểu vừa chỉ ra những thách thức quy mô lớn chưa giải quyết để xác định thái độ hoài nghi có cơ sở (Genuinely curious but skeptical).

Tiếp theo, áp dụng kỹ thuật đọc quét cho các câu hỏi **Chi tiết** (R3Q2, R3Q4, R3Q8) và câu **Loại trừ** (R3Q6). parts.title: Cryptocurrency and Its Shadow Economy of Harm
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Not only has cryptocurrency attracted enormous capital over the past decade, but it has also drawn a cluster of associated harms that critics increasingly describe, with varying degrees of confidence, as a distinct category of technology-enabled vice. Whether these harms stem primarily from the underlying technology itself or from the speculative culture that has grown up around it remains a matter of genuine scholarly disagreement, one that this discussion does not claim to resolve so much as to map.

Trading platforms designed to be used from a smartphone at any hour arguably share more design features with gambling applications than early cryptocurrency advocates might care to admit, a resemblance that some researchers argue is deliberate rather than incidental. Features such as constant price notifications, streak-based rewards for frequent trading, and leaderboards ranking the most active users may not, by themselves, prove that platforms are engineered to encourage compulsive behavior, yet their cumulative effect on user psychology tends to mirror patterns long documented in behavioral-addiction research, even if the underlying mechanism differs from that of a slot machine.

Fraud tied to cryptocurrency has grown increasingly sophisticated, and one particular pattern — sometimes called 'pig butchering,' after the practice of fattening an animal before slaughter — illustrates how thoroughly criminal networks have adapted older confidence-scam techniques to a digital, borderless asset class. Victims are typically cultivated over weeks or months through what appears to be a genuine romantic or friendly relationship, only to be persuaded, once trust is established, to move increasingly large sums into a fraudulent trading platform that displays fabricated gains to encourage further investment. That such schemes can operate across several countries simultaneously, often coordinated by networks that themselves employ trafficked labor, suggests that the harm extends well beyond individual financial loss.

Energy consumption represents another contested dimension of the debate, though the picture here resists easy generalization. Blockchains that rely on 'proof-of-work' validation, historically the dominant model, consume electricity on a scale comparable to that of some mid-sized countries, a fact regularly cited by critics; newer 'proof-of-stake' systems, however, reduce energy use by a factor that some technical estimates place above ninety-nine percent, which complicates any claim that cryptocurrency is inherently energy-intensive as a category rather than as a consequence of specific design choices some networks happen to retain.

Concerns about money laundering follow a similarly uneven pattern. Blockchain analysis firms have found that illicit transactions, while real and non-trivial in absolute terms, constitute a comparatively small share of total cryptocurrency activity when measured as a percentage — a finding that complicates, without entirely undermining, the popular perception that digital assets are uniquely favored by criminal enterprises rather than merely one channel among several that criminals happen to use.

Regulatory responses have varied considerably, from outright bans in some jurisdictions to detailed licensing regimes in others, and the evidence on which approach most effectively reduces consumer harm remains **preliminary** at best. Regulators in several countries have begun requiring exchanges to verify user identities and monitor for suspicious trading patterns, measures that appear, based on early data, to reduce certain categories of fraud without eliminating **them**, though it is not yet clear whether more sophisticated scam operations are simply adapting faster than the rules can be updated.

Taken together, these threads suggest that cryptocurrency's associated harms are neither a fabrication invented by skeptics nor an inevitable feature of the technology itself, but rather an emergent property of how a genuinely novel financial instrument has intersected with existing patterns of fraud, addiction, and regulatory lag. Whether future design choices and policy interventions can meaningfully separate the technology's legitimate uses from its exploitative applications remains, for now, an open question rather than a settled prediction.

parts.title: The Plastic Problem
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Plastic has become one of the most common materials in modern life. It is cheap to produce, light to carry, and easy to shape into almost any form, so factories use it to make everything from food containers and toys to medical tools and car parts. Global plastic production has grown enormously since the middle of the twentieth century. In 1950, factories worldwide made about two million tons of plastic; today that figure has climbed past four hundred million tons a year, and it continues to rise as more industries switch to plastic parts.

A large share of this plastic does not stay in use for long. Packaging, bags, and bottles are often thrown away within days or even minutes of purchase, yet the material itself is remarkably **durable** and can survive in the environment for centuries. Scientists estimate that around eight million tons of plastic waste enter the world's oceans every year, carried by rivers, wind, and careless disposal near coastlines. Food residue left inside packaging before it is thrown away also makes the material more difficult to recycle once it reaches a processing plant. Once in the water, larger pieces slowly break apart into microplastics — fragments smaller than five millimetres — which fish and seabirds frequently mistake for food.

Recycling is often presented as the main answer to plastic waste, but the process is harder than it sounds. Studies suggest that only about nine percent of all the plastic ever produced has actually been recycled; most of the rest has been burned, buried in landfills, or discarded directly into nature. One major **obstacle** is that many products combine several different types of plastic, and these types cannot be melted down together without weakening the final material. Because of this, workers must sort plastic carefully by type before it can be processed at all.

In response to these problems, governments and companies have begun exploring alternatives. Some countries have banned single-use plastic bags and straws, forcing shops to offer paper or cloth options instead. Even though customers sometimes complain about the change, most environmental groups argue that **this** represents real progress toward reducing overall waste. The sorting equipment needed to separate different types of plastic is also expensive, and many local governments simply cannot afford to install it, so some communities send their collected plastic abroad instead, where it may still end up in open dumps. Scientists are also developing bioplastics made from corn starch or seaweed, which break down naturally within months rather than centuries.

Plastic is unlikely to disappear from everyday life anytime soon, since it remains cheaper and more useful than most substitutes available today. However, small changes — from carrying reusable bags to supporting stronger recycling programs — can significantly slow the flow of waste into rivers and oceans, giving both wildlife and future generations a cleaner environment to live in.

parts.title: The Rise of Solar Power
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Although coal and natural gas still generate most of the world's electricity, solar power has expanded faster than any other energy source over the past decade. The price of photovoltaic panels has fallen by more than eighty percent since 2010, a decline driven largely by manufacturing scale and steady technological refinement. In many regions, these lower costs now allow solar installations to compete directly with fossil fuel plants even without government subsidies, a shift that would have seemed unlikely to most energy analysts only fifteen years ago.

Solar panels generate electricity through a process called the photovoltaic effect, in which sunlight striking a semiconductor material knocks electrons loose and creates an electrical current. Roughly ninety percent of panels sold today rely on silicon, valued for its reliability and low production cost. A newer material called perovskite has drawn strong research interest, since laboratory tests suggest it may eventually push efficiency well beyond silicon's limits; whether perovskite panels can hold **that performance** after years of outdoor heat and moisture, however, remains uncertain.

Global installed solar capacity passed one thousand gigawatts in 2022, and annual additions have continued to grow at double-digit rates ever since. China alone accounts for roughly a third of new installations worldwide, having invested heavily in both domestic solar farms and the manufacturing plants that supply panels to other countries. India and several Southeast Asian nations have followed a similar path more recently, expanding capacity quickly as equipment costs continue to decline.

A basic limitation of solar power is that panels only generate electricity while the sun is shining, and output shifts considerably with weather and season. Grid operators must therefore pair solar farms with battery storage or keep other power sources available to cover gaps in production. Battery prices have fallen alongside panel costs, yet storage large enough to support a regional grid still adds substantial expense, a burden smaller utilities often find difficult to absorb.

Utility-scale solar farms require considerable land, and in some agricultural regions this has put developers and farmers in competition for the same fields. Rooftop installations avoid the problem entirely, since they occupy space that already serves another purpose. Floating arrays, mounted on reservoirs and other bodies of water, offer a related solution: they generate power without converting additional land, and the water beneath can even help keep panels cooler and slightly more efficient.

Manufacturing photovoltaic panels is itself energy- and resource-intensive, drawing on raw materials, including rare minerals whose extraction has raised environmental and labor concerns in mining regions. Critics argue the solar industry cannot be called fully sustainable until it addresses these **upstream** impacts directly. Supporters counter that panels generate far more clean energy over their lifetime than manufacturing consumes, keeping the net effect on carbon emissions strongly positive.

Industry forecasts suggest that solar could become the leading source of new electricity generation capacity worldwide within the next decade, provided that storage technology and grid infrastructure continue to improve at their current pace. Some analysts caution, however, that this **trajectory** depends heavily on sustained government policy support and on international cooperation to secure stable supply chains for raw materials, and that either could slow progress considerably if it falters.

parts.title: Traffic and Mobility: Vietnam in Comparative Perspective
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: While many rapidly urbanizing countries eventually shift the bulk of their commuting from two wheels to four, Vietnam's cities have followed a markedly different path, in which motorbikes remain the dominant means of daily transport even as incomes rise. Motorbikes account for a large majority of registered vehicles in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, **a** pattern that sets Vietnam apart from most regional neighbors, where car ownership has expanded far more quickly relative to population growth.

This **divergence** is rooted partly in history and partly in economics. Motorbikes became affordable in Vietnam decades before cars did, and the narrow streets of many older urban districts were never designed for heavy four-wheeled traffic. Even as household incomes have climbed, the relative cost of owning a car — including import tariffs considerably higher than in several neighboring economies — has kept ownership out of reach for many urban households.

Other countries facing similar space constraints have pursued different solutions. The Netherlands invested heavily in cycling infrastructure decades ago, so that bicycles now account for a substantial share of urban trips in cities such as Amsterdam. Singapore addressed congestion primarily through pricing, requiring drivers to bid for a certificate before registering a car, while expanding a rail network extensive enough to make private ownership unnecessary for most journeys. Tokyo built one of the world's densest commuter rail systems, around which the city's later growth was organized.

Vietnam's reliance on motorbikes carries costs of its own. Motorbike accidents account for a disproportionate share of road fatalities nationwide, and rush-hour congestion has worsened even as motorbike ownership itself begins to **plateau**, largely because car numbers have started rising from a low base. Air quality monitors in central Hanoi frequently record pollution among the worst of any capital in the region, a problem researchers attribute partly to the sheer density of small engines operating at street level rather than to any single dominant source.

In response, both major cities have invested in urban rail intended to shift trips away from private vehicles. Hanoi's first metro line opened after years of delay, and ridership, while growing, remains modest relative to designed capacity. Ho Chi Minh City has similar ambitions for its own network, though planners caution that rail alone is unlikely to change commuting habits unless paired with restrictions on motorbike use — a step that has proven politically difficult.

Proposals to restrict motorbikes from central districts have circulated for years, and while some officials argue such measures would reduce congestion and pollution, others caution that removing the primary transport for low-income commuters before adequate transit exists could deepen mobility problems instead. Whether restriction would do more good than harm appears to depend heavily on how quickly rail and bus networks can be expanded.

Vietnam's traffic patterns therefore reflect a transitional moment rather than a fixed arrangement. Whether the country eventually converges toward a transit-oriented model, some hybrid arrangement, or a continued motorbike-centered status quo will likely depend less on any single project than on how policymakers balance affordability, convenience, and the costs of congestion.

parts.title: A Walk Through Cúc Phương: What an Old-Growth Forest Still Has to Teach
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Not until a visitor has walked beneath the thousand-year-old trees of Cúc Phương does the sheer scale of Vietnam's oldest national park become fully apparent. Established in 1962 as the country's first protected forest, the park spans roughly twenty-two thousand hectares of limestone terrain across three provinces, sheltering an ecosystem that has, by most scientific accounts, remained largely undisturbed for centuries longer than the park itself has formally existed.

The park's biological richness is difficult to overstate, though quantifying it precisely has proven resistant to consensus among researchers. Estimates of recorded plant species range from just under two thousand to well over twenty-two hundred, a **discrepancy** that likely reflects differences in survey methodology as much as any genuine change in the forest itself. What is less disputed is the park's role as a refuge for the Delacour's langur, a critically endangered primate found almost nowhere else on Earth in meaningful numbers.

That the park has become a center of last resort for several endangered species owes as much to deliberate intervention as to accident of geography. The Endangered Primate Rescue Center, established within Cúc Phương in the 1990s, now houses individuals **confiscated** from illegal wildlife trade alongside animals bred in captivity for eventual, though rarely realized, reintroduction. Conservationists at the center are, by their own admission, cautious about overstating its success; breeding programs have proven far easier to sustain than releasing captive-born primates into habitats capable of supporting them long-term.

For visitors, the park's appeal lies as much in its accessibility as in its remoteness. A network of marked trails allows travelers with only modest hiking experience to reach striking features, including a botanical garden of rare native species and, several kilometers deeper, a cave once inhabited by prehistoric humans whose remains were uncovered there in the 1960s. Guides note that visitors expecting a brief afternoon excursion are often surprised by how demanding the longer trails toward the ancient trees can become, particularly during the humid summer months.

Chief among the park's attractions is a cluster of trees, some reputedly over a thousand years old, reached only after a trek of several hours each way. Whether the oldest specimens truly predate the founding of the Vietnamese state by several centuries, as some guides claim, remains difficult to verify, since reliable dating of living tropical trees this size is notoriously challenging; even so, their girth and height leave little doubt that they have stood through a substantial portion of the region's recorded history.

Growing visitor numbers have brought the park financial sustainability that many protected areas in the region lack, **[1]** yet managers increasingly acknowledge that this popularity carries its own risks. [2] Erosion along the most heavily trafficked trails has accelerated in recent years, **[3]** and some ecologists worry, without yet having conclusive evidence, that disturbance near busy paths may be altering the behavior of wildlife that would otherwise avoid human activity. [4] Balancing continued access against these pressures has become, officials suggest, the defining management challenge of the coming decades.

Cúc Phương therefore occupies an uneasy but instructive position: a forest old enough to have outlasted centuries of change, now dependent for its survival on decisions made within a single generation. Whether current management proves equal to **that task** will likely become clear only gradually, as the coming years reveal whether conservation and tourism can be sustained together rather than at each other's expense.

  - Với **R4Q10**, nhận diện thái độ của tác giả ở đoạn kết: vừa ghi nhận nỗ lực bảo tồn vừa nhìn nhận những thách thức phía trước, thể hiện thái độ lạc quan có thận trọng/dè chừng (cautiously optimistic).

  - Với **R4Q7**, đọc ngược câu trước cụm từ **"that task"** ở đoạn 7 để tìm nhiệm vụ/mục tiêu được nhắc đến (việc đảm bảo sự tồn tại lâu dài của khu rừng - ensuring the forest's survival).

parts.title: School Lunches Around the World
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: School lunch programs look very different depending on where in the world a student happens to attend school. In some countries, lunch is treated almost like a subject in itself, with clear rules about nutrition and presentation. In others, students bring food from home or buy whatever is available nearby, with far less official oversight. These differences reflect not only budgets but also cultural attitudes toward food, health, and childhood. Even within a single country, lunch quality can vary sharply between wealthier and poorer school districts.

In France, school lunch is often a sit-down, multi-course meal, sometimes including a small starter, a main dish, cheese, and fruit, all eaten at a proper table rather than rushed through in a few minutes. In Japan, the lunch program, known as kyushoku, is centrally planned to meet strict nutritional standards, and students themselves often help serve the food and clean up afterward as part of their daily routine. In the United States, lunch is typically served cafeteria-style, and the quality can vary **enormously** from one school district to another depending on local funding. Many other countries fall somewhere between these approaches, mixing central planning with local flexibility.

Well-designed lunch programs offer benefits that go beyond simply filling hungry stomachs. Students who eat a balanced meal in the middle of the day tend to concentrate better during afternoon classes and show fewer behavior problems linked to hunger or blood sugar swings. Subsidized or free lunch programs for children from low-income families also help reduce a source of daily inequality that might otherwise follow some students throughout their entire school career. Teachers in several countries have reported noticeably calmer classrooms after lunch policies were improved. Some schools also invite parents or nutritionists to help design healthier menus.

Despite these benefits, running a good lunch program is genuinely difficult. Tight budgets often force schools to choose between cheaper, less nutritious ingredients and pricier options that meet stricter health guidelines. Food waste is another persistent problem, since students frequently throw away vegetables or other healthy items they simply do not want to eat, even when cafeteria staff have prepared **them** carefully. This waste **undermines** the nutritional goals the meal was originally designed to meet. Balancing nutrition, cost, and student taste preferences remains an ongoing challenge for administrators everywhere.

Around the world, schools continue to experiment with new approaches to lunch, from farm-to-table programs that source ingredients locally to efforts aimed at reducing plastic packaging and food waste. Some schools now involve students directly in planning menus, hoping that a sense of ownership will make healthy options more appealing. What began as a simple matter of feeding hungry children has gradually become tied to broader conversations about health, sustainability, and equal opportunity in education.

parts.title: Jamu and UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: When people think of UNESCO recognition, physical landmarks such as ancient temples or historic city centers often come to mind first. Since 2003, however, UNESCO has also maintained a separate list dedicated to intangible cultural heritage, a category covering living practices, oral traditions, performing arts, and traditional knowledge rather than buildings or monuments. The distinction matters because intangible heritage survives only through people who continue to practice **it**, not through stone or preservation alone.

In late 2023, UNESCO added jamu, an Indonesian tradition of herbal wellness practices, to this intangible heritage list. Jamu refers to a wide range of traditional drinks and remedies made from ingredients such as turmeric, ginger, tamarind, and various local roots and leaves, prepared according to knowledge passed down through generations. For centuries, jamu has been part of daily life across much of Indonesia, used both to maintain general wellness and to treat specific minor ailments.

The practice of making and selling jamu has historically been closely associated with women. A well-known group of traveling sellers, called jamu gendong, once carried baskets of bottled jamu on their backs and sold it door to door in villages and city neighborhoods. Beyond the physical preparation of the drinks, jamu is tied to a broader philosophy of balance between body, mind, and daily life, reflecting ideas about wellness that predate modern medicine in the region.

UNESCO recognition carries several potential benefits for a tradition like jamu. International visibility can boost tourism interest and encourage younger Indonesians to take renewed pride in a practice sometimes seen as old-fashioned compared with modern pharmaceuticals. Government agencies and cultural organizations often use such recognition to justify funding for documentation projects, training programs, and efforts to support the practitioners who keep the tradition alive day to day.

The recognition also carries risks that specialists in cultural heritage frequently point out. Increased commercial interest can push producers toward mass-produced, standardized versions of jamu that prioritize shelf life and marketability over the more varied, personalized recipes traditionally passed down within families and local communities. Some heritage experts worry that international attention, if not managed carefully, can end up **flattening** the very diversity that made a tradition worth recognizing in the first place.

This tension is not unique to jamu. Many other traditions on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, from traditional music forms to specific culinary practices in various countries, face similar pressures once they gain international attention. Because intangible heritage depends entirely on active practitioners rather than a fixed physical structure, it remains inherently more **fragile** than a monument, which will still stand whether or not anyone visits it.

For jamu specifically, sustaining the tradition will likely depend less on the UNESCO designation itself and more on whether younger generations continue learning the practice directly from elders. Encountering jamu only as a bottled product on a store shelf is not the same as learning the tradition firsthand. International recognition can open doors and draw attention, but keeping a living tradition genuinely alive still depends on the everyday choices of the communities that practice it.

parts.title: Beyond the Horned Helmet: Who the Vikings Really Were
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Popular culture has long portrayed the Vikings as little more than savage raiders, sweeping down from Scandinavia in horned helmets to pillage coastal villages before vanishing back across the sea. This image, while dramatic, badly oversimplifies a culture that was also deeply engaged in trade, exploration, craftsmanship, and even early forms of self-governance. The raiding certainly happened, but it was only one part of a much larger and more complicated picture.

The horned helmet, in particular, appears to be a nineteenth-century invention rather than a historical fact. No archaeological excavation has ever recovered a Viking-era helmet fitted with horns, and most surviving helmets from the period are notably plain, practical pieces of metalwork. Historians generally trace the horned image to costume designers working on operas and later illustrations, whose visually striking choice simply stuck in the popular imagination far more firmly than the archaeological record ever did.

Trade, not just raiding, connected Viking communities to a surprisingly wide world. Norse traders traveled extensively along Russian rivers, exchanging furs, amber, and slaves for silver coins that originated as far away as Baghdad, evidence of indirect but real commercial links stretching deep into the Islamic world. Viking merchants also maintained trading contacts with Constantinople, sometimes serving as elite guards for the Byzantine emperor, a role that placed former raiders in surprisingly formal, institutional positions.

Viking exploration pushed even further than their trade routes, reaching across the North Atlantic centuries before other Europeans attempted similar voyages. Norse settlers established colonies in Iceland and later Greenland, and archaeological evidence at a site called L'Anse aux Meadows, in present-day Newfoundland, confirms that Vikings reached North America roughly five hundred years before Columbus's better-known voyage, though historians still debate how long the Vikings maintained **it** as a permanent foothold. These settlements depended heavily on skilled shipbuilding, since the longship's shallow draft and flexible hull made such long ocean crossings genuinely **feasible**.

Viking society also included forms of collective decision-making that complicate the stereotype of pure lawlessness. Local and regional assemblies, known as things, brought free men together to settle disputes, pass judgments, and make certain communal decisions, functioning as an early and admittedly limited form of representative governance. Iceland's assembly, the Althing, is often cited as one of the oldest continuously operating parliamentary institutions in the world, tracing its origins back to the late ninth century.

The Viking Age eventually wound down for several overlapping reasons rather than any single cause. The gradual spread of Christianity across Scandinavia reshaped political and religious structures that had previously favored raiding expeditions. Around the same period, a cooling climate made the Greenland settlements increasingly difficult to sustain, contributing to their eventual abandonment centuries later. Growing political consolidation into more centralized kingdoms further reduced the loose, opportunistic conditions that had once made large-scale raiding relatively easy to organize.

Taken together, the archaeological and historical record paints a picture considerably more **layered** than the horned-helmet stereotype suggests. Vikings were raiders, certainly, but they were also traders, explorers, craftsmen, and, in their own limited way, early practitioners of assembly-based governance. Reducing them to a single violent caricature flattens a culture whose actual reach and complexity continue to surprise historians studying the period today.

parts.title: Opening Doors: The United States and Trade with Asia
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: By the middle of the nineteenth century, American merchants and policymakers had grown increasingly frustrated by how little access they had to markets across East Asia. Japan, in particular, had maintained a policy of near-total isolation for more than two centuries, permitting only strictly limited trade through a single port and largely barring contact with Western nations. American ambitions in the Pacific, driven by a mix of commercial hope and expanding whaling and steamship interests, collided directly with this policy of deliberate **seclusion**.

In 1853, Commodore Matthew Perry sailed a squadron of American warships, popularly remembered as the black ships, into Japanese waters and delivered a formal request that Japan open itself to trade and diplomatic relations. Perry returned the following year with an even larger force, and under this pressure, Japanese officials signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854, formally ending Japan's long period of relative isolation. The treaty itself granted only limited trading rights, but it opened a door that had been firmly shut for generations.

American motivations behind this pressure were not purely commercial. Steamships crossing the Pacific needed reliable coaling stations, and American whaling crews, who frequently found themselves shipwrecked along the Japanese coast, needed guaranteed protection and assistance rather than the harsh treatment some had previously received. Broader commercial ambition mattered too, however, since American traders hoped that access to Japan might eventually open a path toward the much larger and more lucrative markets of China.

The treaties that followed Perry's expedition, along with similar agreements the Western powers extracted from China during roughly the same period, followed a strikingly similar and one-sided pattern. Provisions for extraterritoriality allowed foreign citizens accused of crimes to be tried under their own country's laws rather than local ones. Fixed low tariffs, meanwhile, limited how much these nations could tax foreign imports on their own soil. Most-favored-nation clauses further ensured that any concession granted to one Western power automatically extended to all the others as well.

For Japan specifically, the consequences of this forced opening proved genuinely transformative, though hardly in ways foreign negotiators had anticipated or intended. Domestic political upheaval, partly triggered by resentment over the unequal treaties, contributed to the collapse of the shogunate and the restoration of imperial rule in 1868. The new Meiji government pursued rapid, deliberate modernization along largely Western lines, driven substantially by a determination to renegotiate the unequal treaties from a position of far greater strength.

China's experience during this same period followed a related but distinct trajectory. Western powers, including the United States, secured a growing network of treaty ports along the Chinese coast. By the century's end, American policymakers had begun formally advocating what became known as the Open Door Policy. This approach was meant to preserve broad, roughly equal commercial access for all foreign powers, rather than allowing any single nation exclusive control over Chinese markets.

Historians continue to debate how best to characterize this entire era of American engagement with Asia. Some frame **it** primarily as a straightforward, if occasionally **coercive**, expansion of global commerce that ultimately benefited all parties involved. Others emphasize the coercive gunboat diplomacy at its foundation, arguing that celebratory language about opening markets obscures how much of this economic access was extracted under direct or implied military threat. Such critics maintain that little of it was freely negotiated in good faith.

parts.title: The Rise of Self-Care
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: In recent years, the term self-care has become one of the most commonly used phrases in conversations about health and wellbeing. In simple terms, self-care means taking deliberate steps to protect your own physical and mental health, rather than waiting until you become sick or exhausted to make a change. Although the idea itself is not new, the word has spread quickly through social media, magazines, and daily conversation, especially among young adults balancing work, study, and personal life.

Self-care can take many different forms, and there is no single correct way to practice it. For some people, it means getting enough sleep every night, eating regular meals, or going for a walk outside instead of staying indoors all day. For others, it involves quieter mental habits, such as writing in a journal, spending time alone, or simply learning to say no to requests that feel overwhelming. Doctors and psychologists generally agree that these small, everyday habits, when practiced consistently, can play an **essential** role in preventing stress from building up over time.

The growing popularity of self-care is closely connected to modern life itself. Many people today report feeling more pressure than in the past, whether from demanding jobs, constant phone notifications, or the need to always appear busy and successful online. During difficult periods, such as the years affected by the global pandemic, interest in self-care increased sharply, as people spent more time at home and began paying closer attention to their own emotional needs. Social media influencers also helped spread the idea, often sharing their personal routines with millions of followers.

However, not everyone views this trend positively. Some critics argue that self-care has become heavily **commercialized**, with companies selling expensive candles, skincare products, and retreats under the label of self-care, even though these products are not necessary for good mental health. **This** has led to confusion, since many people now believe that self-care must involve spending money, when in fact some of the most effective habits, like sleeping well or talking to a friend, cost nothing at all. Critics worry that this focus on shopping distracts from the deeper, more difficult work of managing stress.

Despite this criticism, most experts still believe self-care remains a valuable idea when practiced simply and honestly. Rather than buying expensive products, they recommend starting with small, free habits that fit naturally into daily life, such as resting when tired or spending time with supportive friends and family. In the end, real self-care is less about what a person buys and more about the small choices they make every day to protect their own wellbeing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the term self-care generally mean?

options.A: taking deliberate steps to protect physical and mental health
options.B: waiting until a person becomes seriously sick to change
options.C: spending money on relaxing products and various services
options.D: following daily routines shared by popular social media influencers

questions.explanation: Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét). Tìm cụm từ "self-care" ngay ở đoạn 1. Bài đọc định nghĩa trực tiếp self-care nghĩa là thực hiện các bước chủ động để bảo vệ sức khỏe thể chất và tinh thần thay vì đợi đến khi bị bệnh hay kiệt sức. Do đó, cần chú ý đến các cụm từ thể hiện sự chủ động bảo vệ bản thân.

questions.stem: The word "essential" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: temporary
options.B: confusing
options.C: necessary
options.D: optional

questions.explanation: từ "essential" ở đoạn 2 mô tả vai trò của các thói quen nhỏ hàng ngày trong việc ngăn ngừa căng thẳng tích tụ. Trong ngữ cảnh này, từ mang ý nghĩa vô cùng quan trọng, không thể thiếu cho sức khỏe tâm trí.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Self-care became popular during the pandemic as people paid more attention to mental health.
options.B: Self-care is a popular practice for health, though criticized for its commercialization.
options.C: Self-care mainly involves small everyday habits that help prevent long-term daily stress.
options.D: Self-care has lost its real meaning because companies use it to promote expensive goods.

questions.explanation: Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu chủ đề của các đoạn: đoạn 1 & 2 giới thiệu định nghĩa và vai trò tích cực của self-care; đoạn 3 lý giải sự phổ biến trong đời sống hiện đại và đại dịch; đoạn 4 đưa ra các góc nhìn phản bác về sự thương mại hóa; đoạn 5 tổng kết khẳng định giá trị cốt lõi của nó nếu được thực hành đúng cách. Ý chính toàn bài phải bao quát được cả khía cạnh phổ biến, lợi ích lẫn những lời phê bình về mặt thương mại hóa.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a form of self-care?

options.A: attending a weekly therapy session
options.B: writing in a personal journal
options.C: going for a walk outdoors
options.D: getting enough sleep every night

questions.explanation: Đọc quét danh sách các hình thức self-care được liệt kê trong bài: ngủ đủ giấc, ăn uống điều độ, đi dạo ngoài trời, viết nhật ký, dành thời gian một mình, biết từ chối yêu cầu quá tải (đoạn 2), nghỉ ngơi khi mệt, trò chuyện với bạn bè/gia đình (đoạn 5). Hãy đối soát từng phương án để tìm ra hoạt động không hề được đề cập trong danh sách này.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happened to interest in self-care during the global pandemic?

options.A: it decreased sharply as people focused on work instead
options.B: it disappeared completely once people returned to offices
options.C: it increased sharply as people paid more attention to emotions
options.D: it remained exactly the same as in previous years

questions.explanation: định vị từ khóa "global pandemic" ở đoạn 3. Bài đọc nêu rõ trong thời gian đại dịch, mức độ quan tâm đến self-care đã tăng vọt do mọi người ở nhà nhiều hơn và chú ý hơn đến nhu cầu cảm xúc của mình.

questions.stem: The word "This" at the start of paragraph 4's second sentence refers to _______.

options.A: companies selling products under the self-care label
options.B: social media influencers sharing routines
options.C: doctors' agreement about daily habits
options.D: the pandemic's effect on emotional needs

questions.explanation: Tập trung vào đại từ chỉ định "This" ở đầu câu thứ hai của đoạn 4. Áp dụng quy tắc đọc ngược lại câu phía trước: câu thứ nhất đề cập đến việc các công ty bán những sản phẩm xa xỉ gắn nhãn self-care (sự thương mại hóa/bán hàng của các doanh nghiệp). Từ "This" đóng vai trò quy chiếu cho toàn bộ hành động thương mại hóa sản phẩm này.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do critics say self-care spending distracts from?

options.A: the pandemic's long-term effect on the economy
options.B: the deeper, more difficult work of managing stress
options.C: the importance of following influencers' daily routines
options.D: the need to buy more effective skincare products

questions.explanation: tìm từ khóa "critics" hoặc "distracts" ở đoạn 4. Tác giả nêu rõ các nhà phê bình lo ngại việc quá tập trung vào mua sắm đồ đạc sẽ làm xao nhãng khỏi công việc gốc rễ, khó khăn hơn là việc kiểm soát và quản lý căng thẳng.

questions.stem: The word "commercialized" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: confirmed
options.B: marketed
options.C: forgotten
options.D: simplified

questions.explanation: từ "commercialized" ở đoạn 4 gắn liền với việc các công ty bán nến đắt tiền, sản phẩm chăm sóc da và các chuyến nghỉ dưỡng dưới nhãn dán self-care. Ngữ cảnh này chỉ ra xu hướng biến một khái niệm thành hàng hóa để tiếp thị và kinh doanh kiếm lời.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author most likely believes _______.

options.A: meaningful self-care does not require spending money to be genuinely effective
options.B: buying expensive products is the only reliable way to reduce daily stress effectively
options.C: self-care lost all its value once companies began selling related products for profit
options.D: social media influencers give the most accurate advice available on self-care today

questions.explanation: Kết hợp thông tin ở đoạn 4 và đoạn 5. Tác giả nhấn mạnh những thói quen hiệu quả nhất như ngủ tốt hay nói chuyện với bạn bè hoàn toàn miễn phí, và khuyên nên bắt đầu bằng các thói quen nhỏ không tốn tiền. Từ đó suy luận được quan điểm của tác giả về mối quan hệ giữa chi phí tài chính và hiệu quả thực sự của chăm sóc bản thân.

questions.stem: What is the author's overall attitude toward the self-care trend?

options.A: Objective and balanced, recognizing its real benefits despite existing criticism.
options.B: Strongly negative, treating it as an effective commercial marketing scheme.
options.C: Purely promotional, actively encouraging readers to buy wellness items online.
options.D: Completely indifferent, presenting basic facts without showing any clear opinion. Reading

Cách tiếp cận này thể hiện quan điểm nhìn nhận hai chiều, công bằng và khách quan. Lời khuyên: Ưu tiên xử lý nhanh các câu hỏi định vị rõ ràng như Từ vựng (R1Q2, R1Q8) và Quy chiếu (R1Q6).   - Với **R1Q2**, từ **"essential"** ở đoạn 2 mô tả vai trò của các thói quen nhỏ hàng ngày trong việc ngăn ngừa căng thẳng tích tụ. Trong ngữ cảnh này, từ mang ý nghĩa vô cùng quan trọng, không thể thiếu cho sức khỏe tâm trí.
  - Với **R1Q8**, từ **"commercialized"** ở đoạn 4 gắn liền với việc các công ty bán nến đắt tiền, sản phẩm chăm sóc da và các chuyến nghỉ dưỡng dưới nhãn dán self-care. Ngữ cảnh này chỉ ra xu hướng biến một khái niệm thành hàng hóa để tiếp thị và kinh doanh kiếm lời.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính (R1Q3):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Skimming** (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu chủ đề của các đoạn: đoạn 1 & 2 giới thiệu định nghĩa và vai trò tích cực của self-care; đoạn 3 lý giải sự phổ biến trong đời sống hiện đại và đại dịch; đoạn 4 đưa ra các góc nhìn phản bác về sự thương mại hóa; đoạn 5 tổng kết khẳng định giá trị cốt lõi của nó nếu được thực hành đúng cách. Ý chính toàn bài phải bao quát được cả khía cạnh phổ biến, lợi ích lẫn những lời phê bình về mặt thương mại hóa.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R1Q4):** Đọc quét danh sách các hình thức self-care được liệt kê trong bài: ngủ đủ giấc, ăn uống điều độ, đi dạo ngoài trời, viết nhật ký, dành thời gian một mình, biết từ chối yêu cầu quá tải (đoạn 2), nghỉ ngơi khi mệt, trò chuyện với bạn bè/gia đình (đoạn 5). Hãy đối soát từng phương án để tìm ra hoạt động không hề được đề cập trong danh sách này.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết theo sự kiện (R1Q5, R1Q7):** Quét các từ khóa cụ thể trong bài đọc:
  - Với **R1Q5**, định vị từ khóa "global pandemic" ở đoạn 3. Bài đọc nêu rõ trong thời gian đại dịch, mức độ quan tâm đến self-care đã tăng vọt do mọi người ở nhà nhiều hơn và chú ý hơn đến nhu cầu cảm xúc của mình.
  - Với **R1Q7**, tìm từ khóa "critics" hoặc "distracts" ở đoạn 4. Tác giả nêu rõ các nhà phê bình lo ngại việc quá tập trung vào mua sắm đồ đạc sẽ làm xao nhãng khỏi công việc gốc rễ, khó khăn hơn là việc kiểm soát và quản lý căng thẳng.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R1Q6):** Tập trung vào đại từ chỉ định **"This"** ở đầu câu thứ hai của đoạn 4. Áp dụng quy tắc đọc ngược lại câu phía trước: câu thứ nhất đề cập đến việc các công ty bán những sản phẩm xa xỉ gắn nhãn self-care (sự thương mại hóa/bán hàng của các doanh nghiệp). Từ "This" đóng vai trò quy chiếu cho toàn bộ hành động thương mại hóa sản phẩm này.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R1Q9):** Kết hợp thông tin ở đoạn 4 và đoạn 5. Tác giả nhấn mạnh những thói quen hiệu quả nhất như ngủ tốt hay nói chuyện với bạn bè hoàn toàn miễn phí, và khuyên nên bắt đầu bằng các thói quen nhỏ không tốn tiền. Từ đó suy luận được quan điểm của tác giả về mối quan hệ giữa chi phí tài chính và hiệu quả thực sự của chăm sóc bản thân.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Thái độ tác giả (R1Q10):** Phân tích giọng văn toàn bài. Tác giả vừa nêu bật lợi ích sức khỏe đã được bác sĩ/chuyên gia thừa nhận, vừa phân tích mặt trái của việc thương mại hóa, cuối cùng kết luận bằng lời khuyên chân thành và hợp lý. Cách tiếp cận này thể hiện quan điểm nhìn nhận hai chiều, công bằng và khách quan. Lời khuyên: Ưu tiên xử lý nhanh các câu hỏi định vị rõ ràng như Từ vựng (R1Q2, R1Q8) và Quy chiếu (R1Q6). Tiếp theo, dùng kỹ năng đọc quét dữ kiện để giải quyết các câu **Chi tiết** (R1Q1, R1Q5, R1Q7) và **Loại trừ** (R1Q4). Sau khi đã nắm vững bố cục và chi tiết nội dung, bạn sẽ dễ dàng chinh phục các câu đòi hỏi tư duy tổng hợp như **Ý chính** (R1Q3), **Suy** luận (R1Q9) và Thái độ tác giả (R1Q10).

parts.title: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping Travel Planning
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Although travel planning has traditionally relied on human expertise — travel agents, guidebooks, word-of-mouth recommendations — a growing share of that responsibility is quietly shifting toward artificial intelligence, even before most travelers have consciously registered the change. AI-powered tools now generate itineraries, compare flight prices, and answer detailed questions about destinations in seconds, a capability that would have required hours of independent research only a few years ago. Whether this shift genuinely improves the quality of travel experiences, however, remains a question travel researchers are only beginning to investigate carefully.

The most visible application of this technology lies in itinerary generation, where AI chatbots can produce a detailed, day-by-day travel plan based on a handful of preferences typed into a simple text box. Users need only specify a destination, budget, and general interests — history, food, outdoor activity — and the system will assemble a schedule that, at first glance, often appears remarkably thorough. Some early adopters report that these tools save considerable planning time, particularly for destinations they know little about, though the accuracy of specific recommendations, especially regarding opening hours or seasonal closures, still varies depending on how recently the underlying data was updated.

A more subtle, and arguably more **consequential**, application involves personalization at scale. Rather than simply generating a static itinerary, some platforms now continuously adjust recommendations based on a traveler's real-time behavior — which suggestions they click, how long they linger on a particular listing, which nearby attractions they search for next. Proponents argue that this responsiveness allows for a genuinely tailored experience, one that adapts as a traveler's interests become clearer over the course of planning. Critics, however, note that this same responsiveness can create a subtle narrowing effect, in which travelers are steered increasingly toward options the algorithm has already determined they will engage with, potentially limiting exposure to destinations outside their established preferences.

Pricing represents another area where AI's influence, while less visible to travelers, may prove significant. Airlines and booking platforms increasingly rely on machine learning models to adjust prices dynamically, taking into account demand patterns, competitor pricing, and, according to some industry analysts, individual browsing behavior. Whether **this last factor** — pricing tailored to an individual user rather than to general market conditions — is actually widespread remains disputed, since companies rarely disclose the specifics of their pricing algorithms, and the practice, if confirmed, would raise clear questions about fairness that regulators in several countries have only recently begun to examine.

Concerns about accuracy extend beyond pricing. Because many AI travel tools generate responses by drawing on patterns in existing text rather than verified, continuously updated databases, they can occasionally produce recommendations that sound **authoritative** but are, in fact, outdated or entirely fabricated — a restaurant that closed years ago, a museum requiring reservations the tool fails to mention, a border procedure that no longer applies. Experienced travelers increasingly describe treating AI-generated itineraries as a useful starting draft rather than a finished plan, cross-checking specific, time-sensitive details against official sources before relying on them.

None of this suggests the technology is without genuine value. For travelers navigating unfamiliar languages, translating menus, signage, and conversations in real time through AI tools has removed a barrier that once required either fluency or a printed phrasebook. Similarly, AI-assisted customer service, when implemented well, can resolve routine booking issues far faster than traditional call centers, freeing human staff to handle more complex problems that genuinely require judgment and empathy.

Taken together, the picture that emerges is neither the effortless travel utopia promised in some marketing material nor the wholesale replacement of human expertise that skeptics sometimes fear. What seems more likely, based on current evidence, is a gradual redistribution of tasks — AI handling the repetitive, data-heavy aspects of planning, while judgment, verification, and the more unpredictable elements of travel continue to depend, for now, on human attention.

parts.title: Rethinking Volcanic Risk
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Public perception of volcanic hazards tends to fixate on the most cinematic scenario — a sudden, explosive eruption burying a city in ash within hours — yet volcanologists increasingly argue that this focus, while understandable, obscures a more complicated and in some respects more consequential picture of how volcanoes actually endanger the populations living near them. The catastrophic eruption remains, statistically, a relatively rare event; the slower, less visually dramatic processes surrounding it, researchers now contend, may account for a comparable or even greater share of long-term harm.

Consider, for instance, the phenomenon of volcanic unrest that never culminates in eruption at all. Many volcanoes display measurable signs of activity — ground deformation, elevated gas emissions, shifts in seismic pattern — that persist for months or years without ever producing the eruption such signals would, under older monitoring frameworks, have been assumed to predict. **[1]** This uncertainty carries its own cost: evacuations, when ordered as a precaution, disrupt agriculture, displace residents, and impose economic strain that can persist regardless of whether an eruption ultimately occurs. **[2]** Whether a given signal of unrest warrants evacuation is consequently not a purely scientific judgment but one that weighs the cost of a false alarm against the cost of an unwarned catastrophe, a calculation that varies considerably depending on local infrastructure and population density. [3]

A related complication concerns the timescale over which volcanic hazard is typically assessed. **[4]** Standard hazard maps, constructed largely from the geological record of past eruptions, implicitly assume that a volcano's future behavior will resemble its documented past, an assumption that, while reasonable as a starting point, has proven inadequate for volcanoes whose eruptive style shifts over centuries in ways the available record does not fully capture. Some volcanoes long classified as low-risk based on centuries of relative quiet have, on renewed geological investigation, revealed evidence of far larger prehistoric eruptions than any recorded in living memory, raising uncomfortable questions about how much confidence such maps genuinely deserve.

Ashfall, though rarely lethal in the direct sense that pyroclastic flows or lava can be, illustrates the danger of underestimating **diffuse** hazards. A moderate eruption can distribute a thin layer of ash across an area vastly larger than any zone typically evacuated, disrupting aviation, contaminating water supplies, and collapsing roofs under accumulated weight in ways that, individually, rarely make headlines but that, in aggregate, can impose costs rivaling those of a more concentrated, dramatic disaster. Insurers and disaster-planning agencies, historically slower to model diffuse hazards than acute ones, have only recently begun incorporating ashfall dispersal modeling into standard risk assessments with the seriousness the phenomenon appears to warrant.

Volcanic gases present a further category of underappreciated risk, one that operates on a timescale distinct from both sudden eruption and gradual ashfall. Communities situated near volcanoes with persistent low-level gas emissions face elevated rates of respiratory illness that develop over years rather than during any single dramatic event, a pattern of harm that resists easy attribution and, consequently, rarely factors into the acute-emergency framing that dominates most public discussion of volcanic risk. Epidemiological studies attempting to isolate this effect from other contributing factors — smoking rates, industrial pollution, general air quality — face considerable methodological difficulty, which may partly explain why the issue receives comparatively little sustained research attention relative to its potential scale.

None of this is to suggest that the dramatic, sudden-onset eruption deserves less scientific or public attention than it currently receives; such events remain capable of causing catastrophic, concentrated loss of life within a matter of hours, and monitoring systems designed to provide early warning of exactly this scenario have, by most accounts, saved a considerable number of lives over the past several decades. The more defensible claim is a narrower one: that a hazard framework calibrated almost entirely around the sudden, cinematic eruption risks systematically undercounting the slower, more diffuse forms of harm that volcanic activity, even absent a major eruption, continues to impose on nearby populations.
