parts.tips_md:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho Part 4 của bài đọc này (chủ đề về quyền pháp lý và quy định giam giữ tù nhân), bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật chi tiết theo từng dạng câu hỏi dưới đây:
- **Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Thái độ tác giả (R4Q1, R4Q10):** Áp dụng kỹ năng **Skimming** (Đọc lướt tổng thể).
  - Với **R4Q1**, đọc đoạn 1 và đoạn 6 để nắm tư tưởng bao trùm: rào cản cốt lõi không nằm ở việc thiếu các tiêu chuẩn quốc tế mà ở khoảng cách thực thi (enforcement gap) không đồng đều giữa các hệ thống pháp luật nội địa.
  - Với **R4Q10**, phân tích giọng văn xuyên suốt bài: tác giả sử dụng lối viết phân tích khách quan, cân bằng (measured and analytical), trình bày các luồng ý kiến trái chiều và thực trạng pháp lý đang phát triển chứ không đứng về một phía hay đưa ra kết luận phiến diện.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết & Nguyên nhân (R4Q2, R4Q6):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Scanning** (Đọc quét từ khóa).
  - Với **R4Q2**, quét tên riêng "Mandela Rules" ở đoạn 1. Các quy tắc này không tự động thành luật áp dụng trực tiếp vì chúng đóng vai trò là hướng dẫn không ràng buộc (non-binding guidance) chứ không phải hiệp ước quốc tế có hiệu lực pháp lý bắt buộc.
  - Với **R4Q6**, quét từ khóa "solitary confinement" hoặc "threshold" ở đoạn 3. Cơ quan quản lý viện dẫn lý do nghiên cứu tâm lý hiếm khi đưa ra ngưỡng tác hại cố định và sự biệt lập ảnh hưởng khác nhau tùy từng cá nhân.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q4):** Sử dụng kỹ năng **Context Clues** (Manh mối ngữ cảnh). Từ **"nominally"** ở đoạn 6 bổ nghĩa cho việc các quy định được đảm bảo "trên danh nghĩa" (trên văn bản) nhưng chưa chắc đã thực thi được trong thực tế (in name but not necessarily in practice).
- **Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu đại từ/cụm từ (R4Q3):** Tập trung vào cụm từ chỉ định **"This gap"** ở đầu đoạn 2. Đọc ngược lại đoạn 1 và câu liền trước: cụm này chỉ sự khác biệt/phân hóa giữa các quốc gia – nơi thì tòa án áp dụng Quy tắc Mandela thành tiền lệ pháp lý, nơi thì từ chối áp dụng.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Chèn câu vào đoạn văn (R4Q8):** Phân tích tính liên kết logic: câu cần chèn đề cập đến "This absence of a fixed threshold...". Cụm "absence of a fixed threshold" (việc thiếu một ngưỡng cố định) nối tiếp trực tiếp sau câu ở vị trí **[3]** (đoạn 3), nơi vừa đề cập rằng nghiên cứu ít khi chỉ ra một ngưỡng tác hại áp dụng chung ("rarely specifies a universally applicable threshold").
- **Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q5):** Đối soát các chỉ trích liên quan đến dữ liệu tái phạm (recidivism data) ở đoạn 5. Chi tiết cho rằng việc này "đã được nhiều tòa án chứng minh là vi phạm trực tiếp các hiệp ước quyền con người quốc tế" hoàn toàn không được nhắc đến trong văn bản.
- **Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q7, R4Q9):** Kết hợp logic ngữ cảnh.
  - Với **R4Q7**, từ đoạn 4 suy luận rằng các nhà chỉ trích lo ngại việc kết hợp cải cách điều kiện giam giữ với cải cách án phạt sẽ làm suy giảm sự ủng hộ chính trị và khiến đề xuất trở nên khó bảo vệ hơn.
  - Với **R4Q9**, từ đoạn 7 suy luận rằng việc thu hẹp sự nhượng bộ của tòa án trong các vụ việc y tế chưa thể coi là xu hướng bền vững vì thực tiễn này còn quá mới và phân bố không đều giữa các khu vực tài phán.
Lời khuyên làm bài: Ưu tiên xử lý trước các câu hỏi quy chiếu, chèn câu và từ vựng (R4Q3, R4Q4, R4Q8). Kế tiếp, hoàn thành nhóm câu hỏi chi tiết, loại trừ và suy luận định vị rõ ràng (**R4Q2, R4Q5, R4Q6, R4Q7, R4Q9**). Sau cùng, tổng hợp mạch tư duy vĩ mô để chọn đáp án chính xác cho câu hỏi ý chính và thái độ tác giả (**R4Q1, R4Q10**).

parts.title: The Mekong Delta Under Climate Pressure
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Stretching across nine provinces in southern Vietnam, the Mekong Delta has long supplied nearly half of the country's rice output and sustains close to seventeen million people who depend on its rivers and canals for their daily livelihoods. Centuries of seasonal flooding once deposited fresh silt across the floodplains every year, keeping the soil fertile without artificial intervention. Now, though, a growing body of research suggests that the disruptions of the past two decades, taken together, may be reshaping the delta more profoundly than any single flood season ever did.

Saltwater intrusion has become the delta's most visible symptom of change, even though it is only one strand of a more tangled cause. Rising sea levels push brine further inland during the dry season, but the problem is **intensified** by dozens of hydropower dams built upstream in recent years, which trap sediment and reduce the freshwater flow that would otherwise push seawater back. In some provinces, salinity now reaches areas that were considered safe for freshwater rice cultivation only a decade ago, forcing local authorities to redraw agricultural zoning maps more frequently than before.

Farmers in the hardest-hit districts have responded unevenly. Some have shifted from rice to shrimp farming, a switch that tends to be more profitable in saline conditions but requires capital many smallholders lack. Others have persisted with rice, absorbing yield losses that, according to provincial agricultural offices, sometimes exceed thirty percent in a single season. A smaller number have simply abandoned their land altogether, a decision that reflects not carelessness but the narrowing of viable options as the growing season shortens each year.

The delta's mangrove forests, which once buffered the coastline against storms and provided nursery habitat for fish and shrimp, have shrunk considerably since the 1990s, partly due to aquaculture expansion and partly due to the same sediment starvation driving saltwater intrusion further inland. Fishermen report that catches of several native species have declined noticeably, though scientists caution that overfishing and habitat loss are difficult to **disentangle** as separate causes. What is clearer is that the ecological cushion the delta once relied upon during extreme weather events is thinner than it was a generation ago.

These pressures have accelerated migration out of the delta, particularly among younger residents who see limited prospects in agriculture. Provincial statistics indicate that outmigration rates in several Mekong districts now exceed the national rural average, with many young people moving to industrial zones near Ho Chi Minh City. **Those** who remain are disproportionately older, and some local officials worry that the loss of working-age labor could, over time, undermine the very adaptation efforts the delta needs most.

Government and international agencies have funded a range of adaptation projects, from sluice gates that regulate salinity to pilot programs promoting salt-tolerant rice varieties. Early results from a handful of these programs appear encouraging, though independent researchers note that pilot success does not always translate into results at scale. Whether the delta's residents can adapt as quickly as the environment is changing around them remains, for now, an open question rather than a settled one.

parts.title: How Generations Diverge in Their Social Media Habits
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Surveys tracking social media use across age groups in recent years reveal a pattern that many marketers have been slow to fully appreciate: it is not merely which platforms people use, but why, that increasingly separates one generation from the next. What looks, on the surface, like simple platform loyalty often conceals a deeper divergence in how different age cohorts define the purpose of being online at all.

Facebook's user base, once synonymous with social media itself, has aged considerably since the platform's early years, and this shift has occurred even as total user numbers have remained relatively stable. Users over forty now make up the fastest-growing segment of Facebook's audience, largely because the platform functions for them as a place to maintain long-term connections with extended family, former classmates, and community groups rather than to discover new content. Younger users, by contrast, tend to treat a Facebook account as something inherited from an earlier internet era rather than a space they actively choose.

Instagram occupies a middle ground generationally, retaining strong engagement among millennials while gradually losing its grip on the youngest teenagers, who increasingly describe the platform as **curated** to the point of feeling inauthentic. The app's algorithm, which prioritizes visually polished content and rewards consistency of posting, tends to favor users who already have some experience building a personal brand, a skill more commonly associated with users in their late twenties and thirties than with those just entering adulthood. Even so, Instagram's messaging feature has quietly become one of its most-used functions across nearly every age group, suggesting that private communication may be doing more to retain users than public posting is.

Snapchat, meanwhile, has carved out a distinct niche among the youngest users, not because its features are unavailable elsewhere, but because its ephemeral format, messages and images that disappear after being viewed, aligns closely with what many teenagers say they want from digital communication: interactions that feel low-stakes and temporary rather than permanent and searchable. Streaks, the app's feature that rewards consecutive days of messaging between friends, have become for some users less a form of entertainment than a low-grade social obligation, one that several surveyed teenagers described as more exhausting than enjoyable, even as they continued to maintain them.

Underlying these platform-specific patterns is a broader generational divide in attitudes toward privacy and self-presentation. Older users tend to treat social media posts as relatively permanent records, worth curating carefully because they may be seen by employers or distant relatives years later; younger users, having grown up with platforms explicitly designed around disappearing content, appear less concerned with permanence and more concerned with controlling exactly who sees a given post in the moment it is shared. **This** does not mean younger users care less about privacy overall, if anything, research suggests the opposite, but rather that they define it differently, as a matter of audience control rather than content longevity.

For advertisers, this generational sorting has practical consequences. Campaigns built around polished, **aspirational** imagery continue to perform well on Instagram among older users, but the same approach frequently underperforms on Snapchat, where audiences respond more favorably to content that looks unedited or spontaneously filmed, even when it is not. Some brands have responded by producing entirely separate creative content for each platform rather than repurposing a single campaign across all three, a costlier strategy that several marketing analysts argue has nonetheless proven necessary.

Whether this generational sorting represents a permanent fracturing of social media use or simply a phase that will shift again as today's teenagers age is not yet clear. What does seem likely, based on the patterns observed so far, is that no single platform is likely to serve every generation equally well again, at least not in the way Facebook once did.

parts.title: Denim's Long Road from Workwear to Wardrobe Staple
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: That a fabric once reserved for miners and railroad workers would, within a century, become one of the most universally worn garments on earth is a trajectory few textile historians would have predicted at its origin. **[1]** The twill weave now associated almost exclusively with jeans traces back to at least two competing lineages, one from the French city of Nîmes, whose "serge de Nîmes" is frequently, though not uncontroversially, cited as the etymological root of "denim," and another from the Italian port of Genoa, where a similar cotton fustian was already being woven and exported to sailors decades earlier.

Popular accounts tend to credit a single inventive moment: Jacob Davis, a tailor working with rivets to reinforce trouser pockets for laborers, approaching Levi Strauss in 1872 because he lacked the funds to patent the technique himself. **[2]** What **this** account tends to compress, however, is that riveted reinforcement solved a problem that had already been partially, if unevenly, addressed by generations of workwear tailors using double-stitching and heavier canvas; the rivet was less a singular breakthrough than the final, patentable refinement of a problem multiple tradespeople had been circling for years.

For roughly seven decades after the 1873 patent, denim trousers remained functionally coded: they signaled manual labor, and outside of mining camps, ranches, and factory floors, they were rarely worn as everyday dress. **[3]** The shift began not in fashion capitals but in Hollywood westerns of the 1930s, where denim's association with rugged frontier masculinity was, somewhat **paradoxically**, romanticized for urban audiences who had never worked a ranch in their lives; the garment's meaning was being rewritten by viewers who encountered it only on screen, not by the laborers who actually wore it daily.

It was the countercultural movements of the 1950s and 1960s that completed denim's symbolic inversion, though the process was neither linear nor universally embraced. Youth subcultures adopted jeans precisely because of their working-class associations, using the garment to signal rejection of the tailored formality favored by an older generation; some schools in the United States responded by explicitly banning jeans from classrooms well into the 1970s, a fact that complicates any narrative suggesting denim's acceptance was smooth or quick. **[4]** By the time designer labels began stitching their names onto back pockets in the late 1970s, the fabric had already completed an unlikely journey from workwear to rebellion to, eventually, luxury.

This final pivot into luxury retailing is where denim's history becomes genuinely difficult to summarize in a single sentence, because two seemingly contradictory trends unfolded simultaneously rather than sequentially. On one hand, mass-market denim became cheaper and more globally standardized as production shifted overseas, particularly to South and Southeast Asia, where labor costs were lower; on the other, a parallel market of premium, small-batch denim emerged, often marketed on the basis of selvedge weaving techniques and raw, unwashed finishing that deliberately imitated the roughness of nineteenth-century workwear. That premium buyers would pay a substantial markup to approximate the discomfort their labor-class predecessors had no choice but to endure is one of the stranger ironies in the fabric's already unlikely history.

Environmental scrutiny of denim production has intensified considerably since the early 2000s, driven largely by revelations about the water intensity of conventional cotton cultivation and the toxicity of certain dyeing and distressing processes, particularly those involving potassium permanganate spraying to achieve a faded look. Some manufacturers have responded with laser-distressing techniques and closed-loop water systems, though independent assessments suggest that these innovations, while genuinely reducing per-garment impact, have not offset the environmental cost of an industry whose overall output has continued to expand rather than contract, meaning that aggregate impact may not have improved even where per-unit impact has.

Whether denim's next transformation will be driven primarily by sustainability pressure, by shifting consumer aesthetics, or by some combination not yet visible from within the industry is a question that even denim historians are reluctant to answer with confidence, given how consistently the fabric's past transformations have defied prediction from those closest to it at the time.

parts.title: Is Homeschooling the Superior Path? The Evidence Resists a Simple Verdict
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Advocacy for homeschooling has, over the past two decades, increasingly leaned on academic outcome data, most prominently studies showing homeschooled students outperforming public school peers on standardized test averages. What such comparisons rarely disclose prominently, however, is that most available data derives from voluntary, self-selected samples, families who choose to submit test scores rather than a randomized or even representative cross-section of the homeschooling population, meaning the observed gap may reflect who chooses to report rather than what homeschooling itself causally produces.

Researchers attempting to correct for this selection problem have arrived at a more qualified picture. Some studies controlling for parental education and household income, both of which correlate independently with homeschooling uptake and with academic performance, find that a meaningful portion, though not necessarily all, of the raw test-score advantage disappears once these variables are accounted for. **This** does not establish that homeschooling confers no benefit; it does suggest that the commonly cited comparison overstates the causal contribution of the educational format itself relative to the socioeconomic circumstances of the families who select into it.

Socialization concerns, long a staple of skeptical commentary, have proven similarly resistant to a tidy conclusion. Early critiques suggesting broad social deficits among homeschooled children have not held up well against more recent, methodologically stronger studies, several of which find comparable or even superior measures of social confidence and community involvement among homeschooled populations, particularly those embedded in active co-op networks. Yet this finding itself carries an important qualifier: the benefit appears concentrated among families with access to such networks, which tend to require financial resources, geographic proximity to other homeschoolers, and parental time availability that not every homeschooling family possesses in equal measure.

A separate and comparatively under-examined dimension concerns curricular breadth rather than test performance or socialization. **[1]** Because homeschooling curricula are, in most jurisdictions, subject to considerably lighter oversight than public school standards, the range of subject exposure varies enormously between households, from families offering instruction that meets or exceeds conventional breadth to a smaller but documented minority providing instruction that regulatory bodies in several states have **flagged** as substantially deficient in core subjects. **[2]** This variance is **[3]** rarely captured by aggregate outcome studies, **[4]** which tend to average across a population whose internal diversity may matter more than its mean.

Advocates and critics alike tend to converge, somewhat unexpectedly, on one point: the quality of homeschooling outcomes appears to depend less on the format itself than on parental capacity, whether measured in time, educational background, or financial resources, to sustain rigorous instruction over many years without the institutional scaffolding that public schools provide by default. Where that capacity is present in abundance, outcomes documented in the research literature are frequently strong; where it is thin or intermittently available, the same literature documents considerably more mixed and, in some flagged cases, concerning results.

This capacity-dependence has a further implication that the outcome-focused debate tends to obscure: because families with greater capacity are also more likely to choose homeschooling in the first place, any comparison between homeschooled and conventionally schooled populations is comparing groups that differ systematically before instruction even begins, not two randomly equivalent groups experiencing different treatments. Some researchers have therefore argued that the more useful question is not whether homeschooling outperforms public schooling on average, but under what specific combinations of resources and oversight it does or does not do so.

None of this settles the debate definitively, nor, based on the trajectory of the research so far, does it seem likely to. What the accumulated evidence does suggest, cautiously, is that the question "is homeschooling the best method" may itself be malformed, presupposing a single answer to a question whose true answer is contingent on family circumstances the aggregate data was never well suited to capture in the first place.

parts.title: One Meal, Two Cities: Dining Customs in Mainland China and Hong Kong
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Visitors expecting a single, uniform "Chinese dining culture" across mainland China and Hong Kong are often surprised by how many small but consistent differences separate the two, differences that trace back not merely to regional cuisine but to divergent social histories that shaped how meals themselves came to be structured and shared. Both regions share a foundational emphasis on communal eating, in which dishes are placed at the center of the table for everyone to share rather than portioned individually, yet the specific etiquette surrounding that shared table has developed along noticeably different paths.

In many mainland Chinese households and restaurants, meal etiquette places considerable emphasis on the host actively serving guests, sometimes placing food directly onto a guest's plate as a gesture of hospitality that a guest is expected to accept graciously rather than decline, even when already full. Hong Kong dining customs, shaped partly by decades of dense urban restaurant culture and faster-paced communal dining in crowded dim sum halls, tend to place somewhat less emphasis on **this active-serving gesture**, with etiquette instead centering more heavily on turn-taking with shared serving utensils and prompt tea-pouring for others at the table before oneself.

Tea service itself illustrates this divergence clearly. While tea accompanies meals throughout both regions, Hong Kong's dim sum tradition has developed an elaborate, semi-**codified** etiquette around tea specifically: tapping two fingers lightly on the table to silently thank someone who has just refilled one's cup, a gesture with origins disputed among food historians but widely practiced today regardless of its precise historical origin, and turning the teapot lid upside down or propping it open to silently signal to serving staff that a refill of hot water is needed. Such conventions, while not entirely absent on the mainland, are considerably less standardized and vary far more by region and restaurant type.

The concept of the shared meal as an occasion for building or reinforcing business and social relationships is prominent in both cultures, but the specific negotiating role that a meal plays differs: in mainland business contexts, a formal banquet frequently precedes serious negotiation, functioning as a relationship-building ritual that must generally be completed before substantive discussion of terms feels appropriate. Hong Kong's faster commercial rhythm, several business etiquette researchers note, more frequently allows a working lunch to double as the venue for both relationship-building and negotiation simultaneously, a pattern some attribute to the city's dense concentration of finance-sector professionals operating under considerably tighter daily schedules.

Seating arrangements at a shared meal likewise carry more procedural weight than casual diners from outside either culture might initially assume. The seat facing the entrance directly, or otherwise designated as the position of highest honor, is customarily reserved for the most senior guest or host, a convention rooted in older ideas about a host's obligation to face potential threats first, and violating this seating order, even unintentionally, can register as a subtle social misstep in more formal settings, though younger diners in both regions report the convention loosening considerably in casual, peer-group dining.

What emerges from these accumulated small differences is not a picture of two entirely separate dining cultures but of a single underlying tradition of **commensality** that has been locally adapted — accelerated, formalized in some respects, loosened in others — by each region's distinct urban rhythm, political history, and social structure, producing customs recognizable to both sides yet subtly, sometimes confusingly, out of step with one another in specific etiquette.

parts.title: The Body as a Layered System: Rethinking Anatomical Organization
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Introductory descriptions of human anatomy tend to present the body as a collection of separate systems — skeletal, muscular, circulatory, nervous — each illustrated in its own textbook diagram, a pedagogical convenience that, while useful for initial learning, has increasingly been questioned by anatomists who argue that this system-by-system framing obscures how thoroughly these structures are functionally interdependent rather than merely co-located within the same body.

Consider the relationship between the skeletal and muscular systems, often introduced as though bones provide passive structural support while muscles do the active work of movement. This framing understates the skeleton's own active physiological role: bone tissue is continuously **remodeled** throughout life, with specialized cells simultaneously breaking down and rebuilding bone matrix in response to mechanical stress, meaning that a bone subjected to regular load-bearing activity develops measurably different density and internal architecture than one that is not — a dynamic, ongoing process rather than the static scaffold implied by most introductory diagrams.

Connective tissue further complicates the neat separation between systems, since tendons, ligaments, and fascia do not belong cleanly to any single system in the conventional teaching framework yet play a role in nearly every movement the body performs. Fascia in particular, a fibrous connective tissue once considered primarily a passive wrapping around muscles, is now understood by some researchers to form a continuous, body-wide network that transmits mechanical force across considerable distances, meaning that tension or restriction in one region can plausibly influence movement patterns in a seemingly unrelated region far from the original site.

The nervous system's relationship to movement likewise resists the simple command-and-response model often presented to beginning students, in which the brain issues a movement instruction that muscles then execute. Considerable movement regulation instead occurs through feedback loops involving specialized sensory receptors embedded within muscles and tendons themselves, which continuously relay information about muscle length, tension, and joint position back to the nervous system, allowing rapid, largely unconscious postural adjustments that occur well before any deliberate, consciously initiated movement correction could take effect.

Circulatory and respiratory function, too, are frequently taught as though blood oxygenation and nutrient delivery were entirely separable processes from the musculoskeletal activity they support, when in practice, sustained physical activity triggers cascading physiological adjustments — increased heart rate, redistributed blood flow toward active muscle tissue, altered breathing depth and rate — that occur through continuous, real-time coordination across systems rather than through any one system operating independently of the others.

What **this more integrated view** suggests, several anatomists now argue, is not that traditional system-based teaching is wrong so much as that it risks leaving students with a durable but misleading mental model — one in which the body's systems are imagined as more **modular** and independently functioning than the underlying physiology actually supports, an impression that becomes increasingly consequential in clinical and rehabilitative contexts, where treating a single system in isolation can overlook compensatory patterns originating elsewhere in this densely interconnected structure.

parts.title: Living Alongside Giants: Reassessing Human Coexistence with Large Animals
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Popular narratives of human history often frame the relationship between people and large animals — elephants, bears, big cats, whales — as a story of straightforward conflict gradually resolved through either extermination or, more recently, conservation-driven protection, a framing that obscures a far messier and more regionally specific historical record than this two-stage story suggests. Long before industrial-scale hunting or modern conservation movements existed, numerous human societies developed sustained, functional coexistence arrangements with large animals that involved neither wholesale removal nor simple protection, but rather intricate, culturally embedded systems of mutual **accommodation**.

Several agricultural communities living near elephant populations, for instance, developed elaborate crop-timing and land-use strategies specifically designed to minimize competition for the same resources during particular seasons, arrangements that required detailed, transmitted ecological knowledge about elephant movement patterns rather than any attempt to exclude the animals from shared territory entirely. Such arrangements were rarely perfectly harmonious — crop damage and occasional serious injury to livestock or people did occur — but researchers studying these historical patterns note that the arrangements persisted for generations precisely because the accommodation, however imperfect, proved more sustainable than the alternative of open, sustained conflict.

What complicates any tidy narrative of harmonious traditional coexistence, however, is that the same historical record shows considerable variation in how differently local communities have valued the large animals sharing their territory, depending heavily on the specific animal's perceived economic threat, symbolic or religious significance, and the community's own subsistence strategy. Communities relying heavily on livestock, for example, developed markedly less tolerant relationships with large predators than communities whose subsistence depended less directly on animals vulnerable to predation, a divergence that undercuts any single generalization about how humans have traditionally regarded large fauna.

Modern conservation efforts attempting to draw on this historical record face a further complication: population densities, land-use patterns, and the economic pressures facing rural communities today differ substantially from the conditions under which many traditional accommodation strategies originally developed, meaning that historical coexistence arrangements cannot simply be reintroduced wholesale as contemporary conservation solutions without accounting for how drastically the surrounding circumstances have since changed. Several conservation researchers caution against romanticizing historical arrangements as a ready-made template, noting that the communities that once practiced them frequently did so under population pressures and land-availability conditions no longer present in the same regions today.

Compensation programs, introduced in several regions as a modern substitute for older accommodation strategies, illustrate **this** complication directly: programs that reimburse farmers for crop damage or livestock loss attributed to large animals have shown considerably variable success, with effectiveness depending heavily on how promptly and reliably compensation is actually paid rather than on the compensation scheme's stated terms alone, since delayed or inconsistently administered payouts have, in several documented cases, eroded local tolerance for large animals even where the underlying compensation policy appeared, on paper, generous.

What emerges from this more granulated historical and contemporary picture is that sustainable coexistence between humans and large animals has never depended on any single, transferable formula, but rather on a locally specific balance among ecological knowledge, economic incentive, and cultural valuation — a balance that must be actively renegotiated as surrounding conditions shift, rather than treated as something a historical precedent alone can permanently secure.

parts.title: The Fine Print of Politeness: Etiquette Variation Across Europe
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Visitors who assume that a single, generalized notion of "European etiquette" can guide them reliably across the continent frequently discover, often through minor but memorable missteps, that etiquette norms considered basic good manners in one country can register as either excessively formal or, conversely, oddly casual in another — a variation that reflects deeper, historically rooted differences in how each culture conceptualizes hierarchy, personal space, and appropriate directness. **[1]** These differences persist despite decades of increased regional travel and economic integration, suggesting that etiquette norms prove considerably more resistant to **homogenization** than many other aspects of daily life.

Forms of address illustrate **this variation** clearly. Several Northern and Western European cultures have, over recent decades, moved toward increasingly informal address even in professional contexts, with first names and the informal second-person pronoun used comfortably between colleagues of markedly different seniority levels shortly after an initial introduction. **[2]** By contrast, several Central and Southern European business cultures retain a more formalized address system considerably longer into a professional relationship, in which switching to informal address is treated as a meaningful social step typically initiated by the more senior party rather than assumed automatically, and doing so prematurely can register as **presumptuous** rather than merely friendly.

Punctuality carries a comparably wide range of cultural weight. In several Northern European business contexts, arriving even a few minutes late to a scheduled meeting is interpreted as a meaningful signal of disrespect toward the other party's time, prompting an explicit apology regardless of the delay's brevity. **[3]** In several Southern and Mediterranean business cultures, by contrast, a modest degree of flexibility around scheduled start times is widely tolerated and rarely requires explicit acknowledgment, a difference that has occasionally produced friction in cross-border business dealings when one party interprets the other's relaxed timing as disrespect rather than as an unremarkable local norm.

Gift-giving customs surrounding hospitality likewise vary in ways that can produce unintentional offense despite good intentions. Certain European cultures attach specific symbolic meaning to particular flowers or numbers of flowers presented as a hosting gift, meanings entirely unrelated to the aesthetic qualities of the gift itself, such that an otherwise generous gesture can inadvertently carry an unintended connotation the giver never intended to convey. **[4]** Similarly, gift-wrapping conventions and the appropriate moment to open a gift — immediately in front of the giver versus privately afterward — differ enough across the continent that guidance appropriate in one country can constitute a minor faux pas in another.

Table manners present a further, frequently underestimated source of cross-cultural friction, since seemingly small habits — which hand is conventionally used for particular utensils, whether hands are expected to remain visible above the table throughout a meal, how directly a host's cooking should be praised or critiqued — vary enough across European dining cultures that etiquette guidance genuinely useful in one country can prove subtly inappropriate, or at minimum conspicuously foreign, in a neighboring one.

What this accumulated variation suggests, more broadly, is that no single etiquette framework travels reliably across the entire European continent, and that the practical skill most valuable to a traveler or business visitor is not the memorization of any universal rulebook but rather an attentiveness to local cues and a willingness to adjust behavior region by region, since even neighboring countries sharing considerable historical and economic connection can diverge substantially in precisely the everyday social conventions that visitors most often assume to be shared.

parts.title: Taekwondo: Between Ancient Roots and Olympic Reinvention
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Long before it became an Olympic sport, taekwondo grew out of martial arts practiced on the Korean peninsula for centuries. Early forms of unarmed combat appeared during the Three Kingdoms period, when soldiers trained to fight without weapons as well as with them. Local kicking and striking games, passed down through villages, blended slowly with military training. By the early twentieth century, many of these older styles had scattered or nearly disappeared under foreign occupation, and only fragments survived in scattered schools.

After Korea regained its independence, several martial arts schools, known as kwans, began teaching their own versions of kicking and striking. Each kwan had its own name, its own uniform, and its own way of ranking students. In 1955, a group of masters met to **unify** these separate styles under a single name and a shared set of rules. **They** chose the word taekwondo, combining characters for foot, fist, and way, to represent the new unified art. This decision helped the sport spread more consistently, and it later became easier for foreign students to learn the same basic techniques regardless of which school they attended.

Taekwondo first appeared at the Olympics as a demonstration sport in 1988, when the Games were held in Seoul. Athletes competed, but their results did not count toward the official medal table. Twelve years later, at the Sydney Olympics in 2000, taekwondo finally became a full medal sport. This recognition gave the art global visibility it had never had before. National federations invested heavily in training programs, and interest surged particularly in countries with little previous history of the sport.

Yet Olympic status brought pressure to change. Early competitions were often criticized as slow and difficult for television audiences to follow, since points were awarded by human judges who sometimes disagreed. To fix this, organizers introduced electronic scoring systems built into the chest protectors, so that a kick of sufficient force automatically registered a point. While this reduced disputes over judging, some coaches argue the new system rewards light, fast kicks over powerful ones, subtly reshaping how athletes train.

Despite these debates, taekwondo now **claims** more than seventy million practitioners in over two hundred countries, according to the World Taekwondo federation. It remains one of the few martial arts with genuinely global reach, taught everywhere from small town gyms to national training centers. Whatever disagreements remain about scoring, the sport's journey from village kicking games to Olympic arenas illustrates how a traditional practice can be reshaped, again and again, without losing its core identity.
