parts.title: Why Children Need Time Outdoors
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Children today spend noticeably less time playing outdoors than their parents did at the same age, and the gap appears to be widening each year. Busy family schedules, more homework, and the constant pull of phones and tablets have all played a part in this shift. Many parents notice the change but are not always sure how much it actually matters for a child's development, especially when indoor activities can look just as engaging from the outside.

Time outdoors supports physical health in several clear ways. Running, climbing, and jumping build strong muscles and bones far more effectively than sitting indoors ever could. Sunlight also helps the body produce vitamin D, a nutrient many indoor children now lack. Outdoor play additionally improves balance and coordination, skills that develop naturally through climbing a tree or riding a bike rather than through any planned exercise routine. Doctors who study childhood fitness often point out that these movement skills, once weak, are surprisingly hard to build back later through formal training alone.

The benefits extend beyond the body. Spending time in green spaces has been linked to lower stress levels in children, even after just twenty or thirty minutes outside. **Unstructured** outdoor play, in particular, seems to support creativity and problem-solving, since children left to invent their own games must constantly negotiate rules, roles, and outcomes without an adult stepping in to organize things for them.

This kind of play also teaches social skills that structured activities rarely provide. When children argue over whose turn it is or how a game should work, they practice **compromise** and conflict resolution in a low-stakes setting. Adults who step in too quickly to settle every dispute may, without meaning to, remove exactly the kind of practice children need most.

Getting children outside more often does not require dramatic changes. Parents can start with something as small as a short walk after dinner or a weekend visit to a nearby park. Schools, too, can extend recess by even ten minutes or hold one class period outside each week. None of **these** steps demands special equipment or a large budget, only a willingness to treat outdoor time as seriously as time spent on schoolwork.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what has contributed to children spending less time outdoors?

options.A: busy schedules, more homework, and the pull of phones and tablets
options.B: stricter school rules, fewer parks, and higher outdoor equipment costs
options.C: colder weather patterns, fewer siblings, and longer school days
options.D: increased traffic danger, fewer parks, and higher city populations

questions.explanation: quét các từ khóa "less time outdoors" ở đoạn 1: bài viết nêu rõ lịch trình bận rộn, nhiều bài tập và sức hút từ điện thoại, máy tính bảng ("busy family schedules, more homework, and the constant pull of phones and tablets") là nguyên nhân.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: The specific vitamin D benefits children gain from being outdoors.
options.B: The overall physical, mental, and social benefits of outdoor time for children.
options.C: How screen time has become the single biggest threat to child health.
options.D: Why every child today suffers from a serious lack of outdoor play.

questions.explanation: Áp dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc tổng quan các đoạn: đoạn 2 nói về thể chất, đoạn 3 & 4 đề cập đến sức khỏe tinh thần và kỹ năng xã hội, đoạn 5 đưa ra giải pháp. Ý khái quát đúng nhất là lợi ích tổng thể về thể chất, tinh thần và xã hội của hoạt động ngoài trời đối với trẻ em.

questions.stem: The word "Unstructured" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: supervised
options.B: competitive
options.C: scheduled
options.D: free-form

questions.explanation: từ "Unstructured" ở đoạn 3 mô tả trò chơi tự do, không theo khuôn mẫu hay kế hoạch cố định (đồng nghĩa với free-form).

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does sunlight help the body produce?

options.A: Sunlight helps the body produce vitamin C instead.
options.B: Sunlight helps the body build stronger muscle tissue.
options.C: Sunlight helps the body produce vitamin D.
options.D: Sunlight helps the body absorb calcium more efficiently.

questions.explanation: quét từ khóa "sunlight" ở đoạn 2: ánh nắng mặt trời giúp cơ thể tạo ra vitamin D ("Sunlight also helps the body produce vitamin D").

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a physical benefit of outdoor play?

options.A: Outdoor play helps improve a child's eyesight over time.
options.B: Outdoor play helps build strong muscles and bones.
options.C: Outdoor play helps the body produce vitamin D naturally.
options.D: Outdoor play helps improve balance and coordination skills.

questions.explanation: Tìm đoạn 2 nơi liệt kê các lợi ích thể chất: cơ xương chắc khỏe, sản sinh vitamin D, cải thiện thăng bằng và sự phối hợp. Chi tiết "cải thiện thị lực của trẻ theo thời gian" không được đề cập trong bài.

questions.stem: The phrase "these steps" in paragraph 5 refers to _______.

options.A: special equipment and budget requirements
options.B: schoolwork and academic requirements
options.C: doctors' recommendations for outdoor fitness
options.D: suggestions for getting children outside more

questions.explanation: Định vị cụm từ "these steps" ở cuối đoạn 5. Đọc các câu trước đó về việc đi dạo ngắn sau bữa tối, đến công viên cuối tuần, hay tăng 10 phút giờ ra ra chơi. Do đó, "these steps" quy chiếu đến các gợi ý để giúp trẻ ra ngoài nhiều hơn.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what may happen when adults step in too quickly to settle children's disputes?

options.A: Children may become more likely to argue with each other overall.
options.B: Children may lose the chance to practice compromise and conflict resolution.
options.C: Children may learn to settle disputes more quickly than adults do.
options.D: Children may develop a stronger dependence on structured group activities.

questions.explanation: quét cụm "Adults who step in too quickly" ở đoạn 4: việc người lớn can thiệp quá nhanh sẽ làm mất cơ hội thực hành thương lượng và giải quyết xung đột của trẻ ("remove exactly the kind of practice children need most").

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the connection between unstructured outdoor play and creativity?

options.A: Negotiating their own rules without adult help may exercise problem-solving skills.
options.B: Unstructured play alone guarantees every child will become highly creative later.
options.C: Children became more creative first, which then led them to prefer unstructured play.
options.D: Time spent in green spaces has been linked to lower stress levels.

questions.explanation: Phân tích lập luận ở đoạn 3: việc trẻ tự đặt ra quy tắc và giải quyết vấn đề mà không có người lớn can thiệp chính là quá trình rèn luyện tư duy sáng tạo và giải quyết vấn đề.

questions.stem: The word "compromise" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: conflict
options.B: silence
options.C: agreement
options.D: victory

questions.explanation: từ "compromise" ở đoạn 4 mang nghĩa thỏa hiệp, tìm tiếng nói chung để đi đến thống nhất (đồng nghĩa với agreement).

questions.stem: What is the author's overall attitude toward increasing the amount of time children spend outdoors?

options.A: Strongly critical of parents who limit their children's screen time unnecessarily.
options.B: Neutral, presenting the research without recommending any specific action.
options.C: Alarmed, warning that today's children face permanent, irreversible health damage.
options.D: Encouraging, urging parents and schools to make outdoor time a priority. Reading

questions.explanation: Đánh giá sắc thái ở đoạn cuối: tác giả khuyến khích các hành động nhỏ từ phụ huynh và nhà trường để đưa trẻ ra ngoài nhiều hơn. Thái độ này mang tính động viên, khuyến khích (Encouraging). Lời khuyên: Hãy ưu tiên làm nhanh các câu hỏi định vị trực tiếp như Từ vựng (R1Q3, R1Q9) và Quy chiếu (R1Q6). Kế tiếp, dùng kỹ năng đọc quét để làm các câu Chi tiết (R1Q1, R1Q4, R1Q7) và Loại trừ (R1Q5). Cuối cùng, tổng hợp logic toàn bài để hoàn thành chính xác nhóm câu hỏi tư duy cao gồm Suy luận (R1Q8), Ý chính (R1Q2) và Thái độ tác giả (R1Q10).

parts.title: The Silk Road and the Spread of an Industry
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: For centuries, silk carried a reputation across Eurasia that few traded goods could match, prized in Rome, India, and Persia despite being produced almost exclusively within Chinese borders. What made this monopoly unusual was not that the finished textile traveled thousands of kilometers along trade routes — plenty of luxury goods did the same — but that the underlying production technique remained **confined** to its point of origin for centuries after the trade route itself had become thoroughly established.

The knowledge required to produce silk extended well beyond weaving alone. Cultivating silkworms demanded a reliable supply of mulberry leaves, careful control of temperature and humidity during the worm's life cycle, and a delicate reeling technique for unwinding cocoons without breaking the continuous filament inside. Chinese authorities, according to several historical accounts, treated the export of silkworm eggs or mulberry seeds as a serious offense, reportedly punishable by death in some periods, reflecting how thoroughly production knowledge, not merely the finished product, was guarded as strategic advantage.

How this closely guarded knowledge eventually reached distant regions remains a subject historians continue to debate, since much of the surviving evidence takes the form of legend rather than verifiable record. One widely repeated account credits a Chinese princess, married into a kingdom near Khotan, with smuggling silkworm eggs westward hidden inside her elaborate headdress, evading border inspection meant to prevent exactly this kind of transfer. A separate tradition attributes silk's later arrival in Byzantium to two monks who reportedly concealed silkworm eggs inside hollow bamboo canes during a return journey from Central Asia.

Whichever account, if either, reflects what actually happened, sericulture's knowledge did eventually **diffuse** westward in stages, first establishing itself in oasis kingdoms along the trade route and considerably later within the Byzantine Empire itself. Once local production became viable, the economic logic that had sustained China's monopoly shifted considerably; regions that had previously imported finished silk at considerable expense could now cultivate their own industry, and the trade's center of gravity gradually redistributed rather than collapsing outright.

This redistribution did not eliminate Chinese silk's continued reputation for quality, nor did it end the trade route's broader economic significance, but it did permanently alter the balance of who controlled a resource once treated as irreplaceable. The episode illustrates a pattern with implications well beyond silk itself: controlling the physical movement of a finished good along a trade route offers considerably less lasting protection than controlling the underlying knowledge required to produce it, since knowledge, once it crosses a border by whatever means, is a good deal harder to recall than merchandise ever was.

This same pattern — a jealously guarded production technique eventually diffusing beyond its point of origin, carried more often by individuals than by official transfer — recurs across the history of several other traded goods, from porcelain to certain dye techniques, though the surviving documentation for these episodes is often no more definitive than it is for silk. What the silk case demonstrates with unusual clarity, however measured against imperfect historical evidence, is how difficult sustained technological exclusivity proves to maintain once a resource has become valuable enough to motivate the risk of smuggling it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what made China's silk monopoly unusual?

options.A: The finished textile itself never actually left Chinese territory at all.
options.B: The production technique remained confined to China long after the route was established.
options.C: The trade route connecting China to Europe had not yet been established.
options.D: Silk was the only luxury good ever traded along the route.

options.B: How legendary smuggling stories became more important than silk's economic history.
options.C: How China's guarded silk-production knowledge eventually spread and reshaped economic control.
options.D: Why every traded good in history eventually loses all its production secrecy.

parts.title: A Slow-Growing Tree and an Unlikely Cure
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Among the many stories behind widely used cancer drugs, few are as improbable as the one behind paclitaxel, better known by its original name, taxol. The compound's origin traces back not to a laboratory but to the bark of an obscure, painfully slow-growing tree scattered through old-growth forests of the Pacific Northwest, a species most botanists before the 1960s would have considered entirely unremarkable.

The discovery emerged from a large-scale United States government program that systematically screened plant samples for compounds with potential anticancer activity, testing tens of thousands of species with no particular expectation that any single one would prove significant. Bark from the Pacific yew, collected almost **incidentally** as part of this broad survey, produced striking results against certain cancer cell lines in laboratory testing, results that took years of further research to confirm and understand.

Confirming the compound's promise, however, immediately exposed a supply problem that the initial excitement had not anticipated. Removing bark from a Pacific yew kills the tree outright, and the species grows with unusual slowness, often requiring well over a century to reach a size worth harvesting at all. Producing enough taxol for clinical trials, let alone eventual widespread treatment, would have required stripping bark from a genuinely enormous number of old-growth trees — trees that, once felled for their bark, could not simply be replanted and harvested again within any clinically useful timeframe.

This supply problem placed cancer patients awaiting treatment in direct, uncomfortable tension with conservationists concerned about old-growth forest habitat, since the Pacific yew's slow growth meant that meeting projected demand through bark harvesting alone risked measurable ecological damage within a matter of years rather than decades. Neither side's concern was straightforwardly wrong, which made the dispute considerably harder to resolve than a simple conflict between commercial interest and environmental protection would have been.

A resolution eventually emerged, though not from bark harvesting at all. Researchers discovered that the needles of the Pacific yew — a renewable part of the tree that regrows without killing it — contained a related compound that could be chemically converted into taxol through a semisynthetic process. **[1]** This finding did not eliminate demand for yew material entirely, since needle harvesting still required substantial plant volume. **[2]** It did, however, remove the requirement that every dose of the drug correspond to a felled, centuries-old tree. [3] Later still, researchers developed methods to produce the needed precursor compound through plant cell culture, reducing dependence on wild-harvested yew material even further. **[4]**

The taxol case is often cited, with some justification, as a rare instance in which a natural-product supply crisis found a genuinely satisfying technical resolution. It would be a mistake, however, to treat **this** outcome as representative of how such conflicts typically resolve; many other compounds discovered through similar bioprospecting efforts have found no comparable semisynthetic route, leaving conservation and medical urgency in a tension that taxol's story, however encouraging, does not by itself resolve for the field as a whole.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did removing bark from a Pacific yew create a serious supply problem?

options.A: Because it kills the tree, which grows too slowly to be replaced quickly.
options.B: Because Pacific yew bark contains too little of the active compound to be useful.
options.C: Because harvesting bark from the tree was made illegal shortly after discovery.
options.D: Because the tree only grows in regions with no accessible transportation routes.

questions.explanation: quét đoạn 3: bóc vỏ cây Pacific yew làm cây chết ("kills the tree outright"), trong khi cây lớn rất chậm nên không thể thay thế kịp thời.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: The specific screening program methods used to test plant samples in the 1960s.
options.B: How taxol's discovery created, then resolved, tension between medical need and conservation.
options.C: How conservationists succeeded in permanently blocking all Pacific yew bark harvesting.
options.D: Why every natural-product drug faces the exact same supply crisis taxol did.

questions.explanation: Áp dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc từ đoạn 1 (phát hiện ra taxol) đến các đoạn giữa (xung đột giữa nhu cầu y tế và bảo tồn) và đoạn kết (giải pháp bán tổng hợp). Ý khái quát đúng nhất là quá trình phát hiện taxol đã tạo ra rồi giải quyết sự căng thẳng giữa nhu cầu chữa bệnh và bảo tồn thiên nhiên.

questions.stem: The word "incidentally" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: accidentally
options.B: deliberately
options.C: successfully
options.D: repeatedly

questions.explanation: từ "incidentally" ở đoạn 2 mô tả việc thu thập mẫu cây một cách tình cờ / ngẫu nhiên trong một khảo sát rộng, đồng nghĩa với tình cờ / vô tình (accidentally).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a step in solving taxol's supply problem?

options.A: Converting a related compound found in yew needles into taxol.
options.B: Genetically modifying the Pacific yew tree to grow at a faster rate.
options.C: Producing the needed precursor compound through plant cell culture.
options.D: Reducing dependence on wild-harvested yew material over time.

questions.explanation: Tìm đoạn 5 nơi đề cập các giải pháp cho nguồn cung: chuyển đổi hợp chất precursor từ lá tằm, nuôi cấy tế bào thực vật (plant cell culture) và giảm phụ thuộc vào vỏ cây hoang dã. Chi tiết "biến đổi gen cây Pacific yew để lớn nhanh hơn" không hề được đề cập.

questions.stem: The phrase "this outcome" in paragraph 6 refers to _______.

options.A: the original bark-harvesting method
options.B: the tension between conservationists and patients
options.C: taxol's eventual semisynthetic resolution
options.D: the plant screening program of the 1960s

questions.explanation: Định vị cụm từ "this outcome" ở đoạn 6. Đọc vế trước để xác định kết quả được đề cập: đó là giải pháp bán tổng hợp (semisynthetic resolution) giúp giải quyết bài toán nguồn cung.

questions.stem: What changed about the relationship between taxol production and old-growth trees once the semisynthetic method was developed?

options.A: Doses no longer required felling centuries-old trees, since needles could be harvested safely.
options.B: Doses still required felling old-growth trees, but at a much slower rate.
options.C: Old-growth trees became entirely irrelevant to taxol production from that point onward.
options.D: Conservationists abandoned their concerns entirely once the semisynthetic method appeared.

questions.explanation: quét đoạn 5 & 6 về phương pháp bán tổng hợp (semisynthetic method): việc thu hoạch lá/kim tằm giúp cây tiếp tục sống, không còn phải đốn hạ những cây cổ thụ hàng trăm năm tuổi.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the applicability of taxol's resolution to other natural-product supply problems?

options.A: Every natural-product supply crisis discovered through bioprospecting has since been fully resolved.
options.B: Conservationists' objections caused researchers to abandon bark harvesting before any solution existed.
options.C: Researchers discovered a related compound in the needles of the Pacific yew tree.

parts.title: Why People Give: The Puzzle of Charitable Behavior
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Standard economic models of rational self-interest predict that voluntary contributions to public goods should collapse toward zero once a group grows large enough, since any individual contributor can enjoy the benefit of others' generosity without personally paying for it — a prediction economists label the free-rider problem. Actual charitable giving violates this prediction so consistently, and across such a wide range of societies, that the persistent gap between theoretical prediction and observed behavior has occupied economists and psychologists for several decades without producing anything resembling full consensus.

One influential explanation, often labeled the warm-glow model, proposes that givers derive direct psychological benefit from the act of giving itself, independent of whatever public good the donation ultimately funds. Under this account, a donor is not merely purchasing a share of some collective outcome but purchasing, in addition, a private and immediate sense of moral satisfaction — a benefit that, crucially, does not diminish as more other people also contribute, which would explain why individual giving does not collapse to zero even in very large donor pools.

A separate line of theory emphasizes reputation and social signaling rather than internal satisfaction. Visible giving — a named donation, a fundraising thermometer displayed publicly, a gala attended by peers — may function partly as a costly signal of wealth, generosity, or trustworthiness to observers whose good opinion the donor has reason to value. This account does not necessarily contradict the warm-glow explanation so much as complicate **it**, since a single donation could plausibly satisfy both motives simultaneously, making the two explanations difficult to cleanly separate through observation of giving behavior alone.

Disentangling these motives experimentally has proven genuinely difficult. Laboratory studies using anonymous dictator games — in which a participant privately decides how much of an endowed sum, if any, to share with an unseen counterpart — consistently find that a substantial share of participants give a meaningfully positive amount, a result that seems to weigh against a purely reputation-based account, since no observer exists to signal to. Critics of this inference, however, note that laboratory anonymity may not register as fully genuine to participants, who may act as though observed even when technically unwatched, which would mean these studies understate rather than eliminate the role reputation plays outside the laboratory.

What has emerged from several decades of this research is not a single winning explanation but a hedged, mixed-motive account: most researchers now accept that warm-glow satisfaction, reputational signaling, and genuine empathy-driven concern for a recipient's welfare all likely contribute to observed giving simultaneously, though the relative weight assigned to each appears to shift considerably depending on donation size, visibility, cause type, and the donor's relationship, if any, to the recipient.

Policy design has, somewhat unevenly, absorbed these theoretical complications. Matching-gift campaigns, which promise to multiply a donor's contribution by some fixed factor, are typically justified on the assumption that donors respond to the increased marginal impact of their gift, a warm-glow-adjacent logic. **[1]** Evidence on matching campaigns' actual effect on total giving is, however, considerably more mixed than the intuitive logic behind them suggests. **[2]** Several field experiments find that matching offers do increase individual contribution size substantially. **[3]** Other studies find that a meaningful share of this increase merely redirects donations that would have occurred anyway, sometimes from other causes or from a slightly later date, rather than expanding a donor's overall generosity in any net sense. [4]

A further complication concerns how far any of these findings generalize beyond the specific populations most frequently studied. The overwhelming majority of experimental giving research draws on participants from a narrow set of wealthy, highly educated, English-speaking societies, and the handful of cross-cultural comparisons that do exist suggest the relative weight of warm-glow, reputational, and empathy-based motives may differ meaningfully across cultural and religious contexts that structure giving quite differently — a limitation the field has begun, cautiously, to acknowledge rather than fully resolve.

None of this constitutes a decisive resolution to the original puzzle. What decades of research have produced is a considerably more **textured** account of charitable behavior than either a purely self-interested or a purely altruistic model could offer on its own — an account that remains, by the field's own admission, an approximation under continued revision rather than a settled conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does the warm-glow model predict that individual giving would not collapse to zero even in large donor pools?

options.A: Because the private satisfaction from giving does not diminish as more people contribute.
options.B: Because larger donor pools always produce proportionally larger public goods overall.
options.C: Because reputational concerns increase automatically as more people observe a donation.
options.D: Because empathy for a specific recipient grows stronger in larger groups.

questions.explanation: quét cụm từ "warm-glow model" ở đoạn 2: mô hình này giải thích rằng sự hài lòng cá nhân (private satisfaction) từ hành động cho đi không bị giảm đi khi có thêm nhiều người đóng góp, giúp việc quyên góp cá nhân không bị giảm về 0.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: The specific design of matching-gift campaigns and their effect on total giving.
options.B: Why giving persistently exceeds what self-interest models predict, and how it is explained.
options.C: How reputation alone fully explains all charitable giving behavior observed in experiments.
options.D: Why every economic prediction about human behavior has been proven wrong by donation research.

questions.explanation: Áp dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu mở đầu đoạn 1 (về sự mâu thuẫn giữa mô hình kinh tế tự lợi và thực tế quyên góp) và theo dõi các giải thích ở các đoạn sau. Ý khái quát là lý giải vì sao sự cho đi luôn vượt quá dự đoán của các mô hình tự lợi và các cách giải thích cho hiện tượng này.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a proposed explanation for charitable giving?

options.A: Warm-glow satisfaction derived directly from the act of giving itself.
options.B: Fear of social punishment imposed on those who fail to give.
options.C: Reputational signaling of wealth, generosity, or trustworthiness to observers.
options.D: Genuine empathy-driven concern for a specific recipient's welfare.

questions.stem: The word "it" in paragraph 3 refers to _______.

options.A: wealth, generosity, or trustworthiness

options.C: a costly signal
options.D: the warm-glow explanation

questions.stem: How do critics interpret the finding that anonymous dictator-game participants still give substantially?

options.A: Critics argue lab anonymity may not feel genuine, understating reputational motives' true role.
options.B: Critics argue the finding definitively proves reputation plays no role in giving.
options.C: Critics argue the finding proves warm-glow satisfaction is the only relevant motive.
options.D: Critics argue dictator games measure empathy more accurately than any other method.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the relative weight of warm-glow, reputational, and empathy-based motives in charitable giving?

options.A: Warm-glow satisfaction has been proven the dominant motive in all documented cases.
options.B: The relative weight of each motive likely varies with size and visibility.
options.C: Donation visibility increased because researchers began favoring reputation-based explanations more.
options.D: Most researchers now accept a mixed-motive account combining several explanations at once.

questions.explanation: Phân tích lập luận ở các đoạn cuối: trọng số tương đối của từng động cơ (warm-glow, danh tiếng, thấu cảm) sẽ thay đổi tùy thuộc vào quy mô và tính công khai/hiển thị của khoản đóng góp.

questions.stem: The word "textured" in paragraph 8 is closest in meaning to _______.

options.A: nuanced
options.B: simplified

questions.explanation: từ "textured" ở đoạn 8 mô tả một cái nhìn nhiều chiều, chi tiết và tinh tế, đồng nghĩa với tinh tế / nhiều sắc thái (nuanced).

questions.stem: What is the author's overall attitude toward the mixed-motive account of charitable giving?

options.A: Fully confident that the mixed-motive account definitively and permanently resolves the puzzle.
options.B: Dismissive, arguing none of the proposed motive theories have any real empirical support.
options.C: Measured, presenting the mixed-motive account as a current approximation rather than a final answer.
options.D: Alarmed, warning that charitable giving research has produced no useful findings whatsoever.
